content.dek: A survey’s two-part taxonomy separates what an agent test measures from how it measures it. One recent tool-use study shows why the distinction matters.

body.heading: Start with the objective and the process
paragraphs: An “agent benchmark” can refer to a test of task completion, tool choice, planning, memory, reliability, or safety. It can also describe a testing process: fixed prompts or interactive tasks, synthetic or real-world data, automated or human scoring, and a controlled simulation or live environment. Collapsing those dimensions into one leaderboard number makes it hard to tell what a result actually covers.

A 2025 survey of LLM-agent evaluation proposes two axes: evaluation objectives and evaluation process. Its objective categories include agent behavior, capabilities, reliability, and safety or alignment. Its process categories include interaction mode, evaluation data, metrics, tooling, and context or environment. The survey notes that agent evaluation differs from static software tests because agents act across dynamic environments, and that enterprise needs such as access control, reliability, auditability, and long-running interaction are not consistently covered by existing work. [@agent-evaluation-survey-2025]

This article uses a two-source qualitative crosswalk: it records the survey’s named dimensions, then maps one primary benchmark’s tasks and reported method against those dimensions. The unit of analysis is the evaluation design and its disclosures, not a model’s relative quality. This is an illustrative literature map, not a systematic review or a new benchmark.

cells: Did the agent complete the user’s task?
Behavior and task completion
Goal definition, environment state, success metric
Did it choose and use tools correctly?
Tool-use capability
Tool set, permissions, interaction trace, error handling
Did it remain reliable across steps?
Reliability and recovery
Repeated runs, failures, retries, persistent constraints
Did it avoid harmful or unauthorized actions?
Safety and alignment
Threat model, policy boundary, human review, scoring
Can another team reproduce the result?
Any objective
Dataset, benchmark version, harness, model and tool configuration

body.heading: A benchmark can isolate one slice of an agent workflow
paragraphs: AgentFloor, a 2026 arXiv preprint, illustrates a specific kind of study rather than a universal test of agent quality. The authors describe a deterministic 30-task benchmark organized into six tiers, ranging from instruction following and tool use to multi-step coordination and long-horizon planning under persistent constraints. They report 16 open-weight models, GPT-5, and 16,542 scored runs. In the abstract, the strongest open-weight model matches GPT-5 in aggregate on this benchmark, while frontier models retain an advantage on long-horizon planning and neither side reaches strong reliability. The authors also report that targeted interventions affect models differently. These are claims about the benchmark and model set the authors evaluated, not a guarantee about production workflows. [@agentfloor-2026]

The AgentFloor example is easier to interpret when its objective is separated from its process. Its objective is to probe the point at which a workflow may need stronger model capability. Its process includes a fixed task set, tiered difficulty, repeated scored runs, and a particular harness. A reader can ask whether the tasks resemble their own work, whether the available tools match their deployment, and whether the scoring captures recovery and verification. If those conditions differ, the result may still be informative, but it does not directly estimate performance in the new setting.

The survey’s taxonomy helps avoid a common category error: using a task-completion rate as if it measured reliability, safety, or cost as well. A task can be completed after an unsafe attempt; a tool call can be correct while the final answer is wrong; a successful run may hide repeated failures; and a fixed benchmark may not test how an agent behaves when its permissions or environment change. Each is a separate question requiring its own evidence.

body.heading: Keep the evidence dimensions attached to the number
paragraphs: For any reported agent result, a reader should record at least the task objective, interaction mode, environment, data or benchmark version, metrics, scoring method, tool access, and model checkpoint. Reliability claims also need to say whether tasks were repeated and how variance was handled. Safety claims need a threat model and an account of whether a human reviewer or an automated judge made the decision. When a result omits one of these fields, the gap limits interpretation; it is not proof that the agent failed that dimension.

This is especially important for enterprise pilots. A benchmark that tests tool selection in a sandbox may not establish that the deployed identity has least privilege, that approval requests reach the right person, or that actions can be audited later. Conversely, a platform’s audit or approval documentation is not evidence that an agent can complete tasks robustly. Evaluation outcomes and deployment controls belong in different rows of an acceptance plan.

The survey is a map of evaluation concepts, not a census of every paper or a current score database. AgentFloor is one preprint example and should not be treated as a representative sample of agent systems. Neither source independently validates the other: the survey organizes evaluation dimensions, while the study reports one designed experiment. A stronger review would code multiple primary benchmarks against the same objective/process rubric and distinguish peer-reviewed evidence from preprints.
**Bottom line:** Agent evaluation is multidimensional; the objective, test process, scoring, and environment must travel with each result.
**Why it matters:** A single benchmark score can hide whether an agent was tested for task success, reliability, safety, or only one capability.

**Key takeaways:** The survey separates what is evaluated from how the evaluation is run. AgentFloor tests a bounded 30-task ladder, not every production workflow. Tool-use capability, long-horizon reliability, and safety are different claims. Missing benchmark details narrow what a result can support.
**What changes:** Evaluation reports should publish the objective, environment, tool set, benchmark version, scoring method, and known exclusions alongside the headline result.

articles.title: Public model cards use different frames for safety evaluation
articles.author: Global AI News Editorial Desk

content_type_status.rationale: The completed draft was checked against the assigned editorial form.

content.dek: Four first-party cards describe safety tests by different domains and methods. Their headings do not create a common safety scale.

body.heading: Compare the evaluation record, not the provider’s safety label
paragraphs: This audit asks how four public model documents describe safety evaluation: Gemma 4, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Grok 4.7. It codes the visible safety domains, evaluation types, ownership cues, and caveats. The goal is to understand what a reader can learn from the documents—not to rank the models or infer that a longer card means a safer system. [@gemma4-model-card] [@gemini38-flash-card] [@claude-sonnet55-system-card] [@grok47-model-card]

The original model-card proposal describes short documents accompanying trained models. It recommends reporting intended-use cases, performance across conditions relevant to application domains, evaluation procedures, and other context that helps users judge suitability. That framework helps explain why test conditions and audience matter: an evaluation result is most useful when readers know what was tested, how it was measured, and where the system may fail. It does not establish one mandatory safety rubric for all providers. [@model-cards-paper-2019]

headers: Safety evidence visible in the reviewed card

cells: Gemma 4
Separate ethics and safety, evaluation approach/results, use, and limitations sections [@gemma4-model-card]
The provider’s evaluation remains first-party evidence
Gemini 3.8 Flash
Automated policy evaluations, multilingual safety results, specialist red teaming, and a frontier-safety assessment [@gemini38-flash-card]
The card distinguishes automated evaluations from human red teaming
Claude Sonnet 5.5
Responsible-scaling, cyber, harmlessness, child-safety, mental-health, bias and integrity, and external-testing sections [@claude-sonnet55-system-card]
Anthropic says some labor-intensive evaluations are omitted and emphasizes numerical results
Grok 4.7
Cyber, biological and chemical, jailbreak, general-output, mental-health, and behavior sections [@grok47-model-card]
Results generally concern the final deployed checkpoint unless a section says otherwise

body.heading: “Safety evaluation” can mean very different tests
paragraphs: Gemini 3.8 Flash’s card says that some safety results are automated development-phase evaluations, not human evaluation or red teaming. It separately describes specialist manual red teaming by teams outside the model-development team. Its multilingual safety table uses percentage-point changes against the preceding model and notes that lower is better for the listed metric. Those distinctions matter: automated policy checks, specialist adversarial work, and a comparative score are not interchangeable forms of evidence. [@gemini38-flash-card]

Claude Sonnet 5.5 presents a wide safety record across multiple sections, including cyber, harmful requests, child safety, mental health, bias and integrity, and external testing. The executive summary says that some evaluations requiring significant human time are omitted and that the card concentrates more on numerical results than extended prose analysis. A reader can therefore see both the breadth of the published program and an explicit boundary on what the public document contains. [@claude-sonnet55-system-card]

Grok 4.7 organizes its disclosure by capability and risk domains, including cyber, biological and chemical capabilities, jailbreak resistance, general output safety, and mental health. The card says evaluation results under those sections generally refer to the final deployed checkpoint unless noted otherwise. This is a useful version statement, but the category structure differs from Anthropic’s or Google’s and does not provide a one-to-one translation between their tests. [@grok47-model-card]

Gemma 4 provides sections for ethics and safety, evaluation approach and results, intended use, and limitations. That gives readers signposts for locating the information, but the presence of a section is not itself a measurement of a safety property. To make a cross-provider claim, an analyst would need aligned task definitions, prompt sets, models, thresholds, and scoring procedures, or independent tests using the same protocol. [@gemma4-model-card]

body.heading: Thresholds and ownership are not a shared scale
paragraphs: A first-party card can report meaningful detail without enabling a valid cross-model comparison. The cards use different safety domains and disclose evaluation ownership with different specificity. One distinguishes automated testing from external red teaming; another has an external-testing section and states that some tests are omitted; another organizes results around risk areas and a deployed checkpoint. [@gemini38-flash-card] [@claude-sonnet55-system-card] [@grok47-model-card] A reader cannot infer that a provider with more headings tested more thoroughly, or that a reported percentage uses the same denominator as another publisher’s percentage.

Thresholds require the same care. A document may describe a named safety threshold for one capability or a comparison against an earlier model. [@gemini38-flash-card] [@claude-sonnet55-system-card] [@grok47-model-card] That does not mean another document uses the same threshold, task, or decision rule. This audit therefore records whether a card identifies a method, test owner, model checkpoint, and limitation, while leaving raw scores in their original context. It does not normalize results or calculate a composite “safety score.”

The strongest supported conclusion is about disclosure structure: these four cards expose different slices of the evaluation process. [@gemma4-model-card] [@gemini38-flash-card] [@claude-sonnet55-system-card] [@grok47-model-card] The source set is first-party and selected, so it cannot establish which provider has the safest product or whether unpublished tests exist. An independent comparison would need a common test suite, shared evaluation settings, clear threat boundaries, multiple runs where appropriate, and disclosure of failures as well as successes.

For each published result, keep the denominator and tested checkpoint with the score, and mark undisclosed fields as “not reported” rather than treating them as zero or as a failed test. This preserves the boundary between absent documentation and negative evidence.

When two cards use the same label, compare its definition before comparing the score. Keep each provider’s category and denominator intact; if either is missing, mark the comparison unresolved rather than translating both results into a shared “safe” or “pass” rating.
**Bottom line:** Public safety cards describe different domains, test types, and caveats; their results should not be collapsed into a single cross-provider ranking.
**Why it matters:** Safety claims are meaningful only when readers can see the checkpoint, test method, ownership, and limitations behind them.

**Key takeaways:** Automated checks, external testing, specialist red teaming, and provider self-report are distinct. The cards use different safety categories and do not share a universal threshold. A section heading does not prove that a test covers every relevant risk. These first-party documents are evidence of disclosure, not independent validation.
**What changes:** Model releases should publish stable evaluation protocols, tested checkpoints, scope, thresholds, limitations, and negative findings in a comparable structure.

articles.title: Agent platform documents separate approval, permissions, and audit
articles.author: Global AI News Editorial Desk

content_type_status.rationale: The completed draft was checked against the assigned editorial form.

content.dek: Documentation from four agent platforms describes different control layers. An approval prompt, an access rule, and an audit log solve different problems.

body.heading: Treat “human oversight” as several controls
paragraphs: A buyer evaluating an agent platform may see terms such as human approval, permissions, and audit logs presented together. They are related, but not equivalent. Approval can pause a sensitive action for a person; permission rules determine whether a tool or resource is allowed; audit records help reconstruct what happened. This document audit reviews official guidance from OpenAI’s Agents SDK, Google’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Anthropic’s Claude Code, and LangChain’s LangSmith Fleet, with OWASP’s Agent Control Standard as a project-level reference. It is not a product test. [@openai-agents-hitl-doc] [@google-agent-audit-logging] [@anthropic-claude-code-permissions] [@langsmith-fleet-oversight] [@owasp-agent-control-standard]

headers: What the documentation does not establish

cells: Human approval
OpenAI SDK can pause a run for a tool decision and resume after approve/reject [@openai-agents-hitl-doc]
The SDK guide does not authenticate or authorize the person making the decision
Audit
Google documents Admin Activity, Data Access, and System Event logs [@google-agent-audit-logging]
Logging records activity; the page does not claim that logs prevent the action
Tool permissions
Claude Code provides allow, ask, and deny rules with managed settings and sandbox controls [@anthropic-claude-code-permissions]
These details apply to Claude Code’s coding-agent environment, not every Anthropic model use
Identity and credential scope
LangSmith Fleet describes fixed and user-specific credentials, with role-based and attribute-based access [@langsmith-fleet-oversight]
Product documentation is not a deployment test or proof that an organization configured controls correctly
Runtime policy hooks
OWASP’s Agent Control Standard aims to make agent systems inspectable and policy-enforceable [@owasp-agent-control-standard]
It is project guidance, not a regulation and not evidence of universal implementation

body.heading: Approval is a workflow, not an identity system
paragraphs: The OpenAI Agents SDK documentation describes a human-in-the-loop flow in which a tool can require approval, the run pauses, a pending request is surfaced, and a decision can be applied before the run resumes. Its documentation also covers persisting and resuming run state. But the guide explicitly puts authentication and authorization of the approver outside the SDK flow: a developer must implement those controls. Serialized state also needs server-side integrity and replay protections. A “human approval” feature therefore does not by itself answer who is allowed to approve, whether the decision matches the request, or how it is protected in a web application. [@openai-agents-hitl-doc]

Claude Code’s permission documentation describes a different layer: rule-based decisions about tools and actions. Its modes range from prompting on a tool’s first use to read-only planning, automatically accepting file edits, and skipping permission prompts; matching rules are evaluated in deny, ask, then allow order. Managed settings and operating-system sandboxing add further boundaries. These are concrete controls for the coding assistant, but readers should not generalize them to all agents built with Anthropic models. [@anthropic-claude-code-permissions]

body.heading: Audit records explain activity after or during an action
paragraphs: Google’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform audit page describes three log categories. Admin Activity and System Event logs are always enabled and cannot be disabled; Data Access logs include reads and writes of user data and are disabled by default. The page presents logs as a way to answer who did what, where, and when. That is accountability and investigation evidence. The document does not say those records block a tool call or obtain a human decision before execution. [@google-agent-audit-logging]

LangSmith Fleet’s page describes tiered permissions, credential management, human-in-the-loop oversight, and an audit trail. It distinguishes fixed credentials shared by an agent from user credentials that act on behalf of the invoking person, and documents tool access control including role-based and attribute-based permissions. That difference is important for delegated work: shared credentials can simplify a team agent but may obscure which individual’s privileges should apply, while user-scoped credentials depend on each person’s authentication and access. The page describes product options, not a security review of any customer configuration. [@langsmith-fleet-oversight]

OWASP’s Agent Control Standard describes an open foundation for exposing middleware hooks and enforcing safety policies at runtime. Its stated goal is inspectable, traceable, instrumentable agent behavior. The source expressly frames the work as a standard project, not a regulation and not proof that platforms implement it. It can help teams ask about interoperable control points, but a standard’s existence does not show that a deployed agent has those controls enabled. [@owasp-agent-control-standard]

body.heading: Build a control map, not a feature checklist
paragraphs: These documents point to different questions for a pilot. Before an action, who can call a tool and with which identity? At the point of execution, what requires approval and can a policy deny it? During the run, what is logged and are data-access logs enabled? After an interruption, how is the state protected and resumed? For a specific product, which settings are defaults, which require an enterprise plan, and which need application code?

A purchase checklist that merely asks “Does the platform have human oversight?” can hide gaps between those steps. An approval gate may not limit what the agent can propose. A permission rule may not record the reason for access. A complete trace may be available only after the event. A project standard may describe hooks without being implemented. Each needs separate evidence and a configuration test in the buyer’s own environment.

The comparison is bounded to public documentation captured for four products and one standard project. It does not inspect source code, test product behavior, confirm current plan availability, or show that a customer’s deployment is configured safely. Documentation can also change. The useful output is a set of questions to verify in a pilot, not a claim that one provider offers stronger security than another.
**Bottom line:** Approval, tool permission, identity, and audit are separate control layers; verify each one in the actual deployment.
**Why it matters:** A visible approval prompt cannot compensate for unclear identity, broad permissions, missing logs, or an unsafe resume path.

**Key takeaways:** The OpenAI SDK pauses and resumes runs but leaves approver authentication to the application. Google’s audit logs record activity; Data Access logging is disabled by default. Claude Code permission modes are product-specific and include distinct allow/ask/deny behavior. OWASP ACS is guidance, not a regulation or proof of implementation.
**What changes:** Pilot plans should test identity, action authorization, approvals, log coverage, and interruption recovery as separate requirements.

articles.title: C2PA 2.1 and 2.4 add different provenance capabilities
articles.author: Global AI News Editorial Desk

content_type_status.rationale: The completed draft was checked against the assigned editorial form.

content.dek: The 2.1 and 2.4 specification records describe changes to assertions, formats, validation, and serialization. A version listing is not evidence of adoption.

body.heading: Read the change record before describing the standard
paragraphs: C2PA versions are often summarized as if a new number meant a single new capability. The official technical specifications show a broader pattern: updates can change how a manifest is represented, what assertions it can carry, how a validator interprets it, and which asset types can embed credentials. This audit compares selected release records for versions 2.1 and 2.4, using the specifications’ own version notes and change summaries. It is not a complete migration analysis. [@c2pa-spec-21] [@c2pa-spec-24]

The 2.1 specification’s version history dates it to September 2024. Its change record clarifies manifest and asset states, deprecation and versioning. It adds the `ingredients v3` assertion, the `c2pa.hash.bmff.v3` assertion, a time-stamp manifest for establishing an asset’s time of existence, and a requirement to validate ingredients when the `ingredients` assertion is used. Separately, the format-embedding section lists JPEG XL support; the change list reviewed here does not identify that format as a new 2.1 addition. These examples affect different parts of the system: assertions describe provenance information, timestamps address temporal evidence, and validation instructions govern interpretation. [@c2pa-spec-21]

The 2.4 version history dates that release to April 2026. Its record adds manifest support for HTML and structured-text formats such as YAML and Markdown, and introduces crJSON, a JSON-LD serialization of a C2PA Manifest Store intended for profile evaluation, interoperability testing, and validation reporting. The version history cautions that crJSON is a derived view over C2PA data, not independently verifiable, and not intended as an input format. The release also adds assertions for repository receipts, environmental-sustainability information, and machine-readable AI disclosure. Other listed changes extend live-video support to dynamically packaged content, add `digitalSourceType` to ingredient assertions, and move where `specVersion` is carried. [@c2pa-spec-24]

headers: Examples in the official change record
Why the change matters to an implementer

cells: September 2024
Manifest and asset-state clarifications; `ingredients v3`; `c2pa.hash.bmff.v3`; time-stamp manifest; ingredient-validation updates [@c2pa-spec-21]
Affects assertion handling, required validation, and time evidence
April 2026
HTML and structured-text embedding; crJSON; repository-receipt, sustainability, and AI-disclosure assertions; live-video and versioning changes [@c2pa-spec-24]
Broadens document and workflow support and adds new machine-readable claims

body.heading: Version numbers do not tell an implementer what is compatible
paragraphs: The table is a selection of notable changes, not a complete diff. C2PA lists versions 2.2 and 2.3 between 2.1 and 2.4; the specification’s own version history dates those releases to May and December 2025. An implementer who compares only 2.1 and 2.4 can miss features or compatibility changes introduced in those intermediate versions. The comparison therefore answers “what do these two records say?” rather than “what is the entire migration path?” [@c2pa-spec-24]

It is also important to distinguish a new assertion from a verified fact about the content. A specification can define how a machine-readable AI-disclosure assertion or repository receipt is represented and validated. It cannot, by itself, prove that every creator adds the assertion, that every viewer checks it, or that the assertion is truthful. The same boundary applies to format support: a specification describing HTML or Markdown embedding does not demonstrate that a particular publisher’s workflow produces or validates those credentials. [@c2pa-spec-24]

The two versions also illustrate why “provenance” is not a single data field. The 2.1 record includes improved state definitions, ingredient handling, and a timestamp manifest; the 2.4 record extends the set of supported assets and assertions and changes parts of the serialization and versioning model. [@c2pa-spec-21] [@c2pa-spec-24] An implementer needs to know which schema version a tool reads, which assertions it understands, and how it treats unknown or deprecated constructs. The change record is a starting point for that review, not a substitute for testing the actual generator and validator.

body.heading: Keep specification capability separate from adoption
paragraphs: This audit does not inspect browser, camera, editing, or publishing products. It cannot estimate how many services implement 2.4, whether older credentials remain valid in a specific tool, or whether a given platform verifies each new assertion. Those questions require implementation documentation, conformance tests, and live interoperability checks. A policy or newsroom article should therefore say “the specification supports” only when describing the normative record, and reserve “the product supports” for a verified implementation source.

The findings are also bounded by the documents selected. The 2.1 specification’s release notes and the 2.4 specification’s change record are primary evidence about their own text, but they are not an independent assessment of whether every change improves security or usability. The article makes no recommendation to upgrade without checking the intervening releases, implementation dependencies, and verifier behavior.

For a practical version review, record the producer and validator versions, the manifest format, assertion names and versions, and the handling of unknown or deprecated items. Then test the same credential through both tools and preserve the validation result. This makes version support observable instead of assuming that a newer specification page guarantees compatible software.
When writing a release note, tie each capability to its version and clause instead of describing the standard as one continuous feature set.
**Bottom line:** C2PA 2.1 and 2.4 document changes across assertions, validation, formats, and serialization; adoption and compatibility require separate evidence.
**Why it matters:** A standards update can change what a credential carries without proving that tools in a publishing workflow implement it.

**Key takeaways:** C2PA 2.1 is dated September 2024; 2.4 is dated April 2026. 2.1 includes state, ingredient, timestamp, validation, and JPEG XL updates. 2.4 adds crJSON, new assertions, and HTML/structured-text support, among other changes. Versions 2.2 and 2.3 sit between the selected snapshots and are not fully audited here.
**What changes:** Implementers should test producer and validator behavior against the exact specification version and assertion set they deploy.

articles.title: What model cards disclose about non-English safety tests
articles.author: Global AI News Editorial Desk

content_type_status.rationale: The completed draft was checked against the assigned editorial form.

content.dek: Four provider documents use different levels of language detail. A language-support count is not the same as a language-specific safety result.

body.heading: Ask what the safety test says about language
paragraphs: A provider may state that a model supports many languages, publish one combined “multilingual” result, or list outcomes for named languages. Those disclosures answer different questions. This audit reviews the language detail visible in four 2026 model documents: Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Gemma 4, and Grok 4.7. It codes whether a page names languages, identifies safety-specific tests, provides a metric, and distinguishes the test from other evaluations. It does not measure model performance in any language. [@gemini38-flash-card] [@claude-sonnet55-system-card] [@gemma4-model-card] [@grok47-model-card]

cells: Claude Sonnet 5.5 system card
Names seven tested languages, including Hindi [@claude-sonnet55-system-card]
Harmful-request evaluations span 16 policy areas and report harmless-response rates
The results do not represent every dialect, language variety, or use context
Gemini 3.8 Flash model card
Describes a multilingual safety metric and non-English performance; the displayed result does not name each language [@gemini38-flash-card]
Automated results are separated from manual specialist red teaming
A combined metric cannot identify which language drove a change
Gemma 4 model card
Says out-of-the-box support covers 35+ languages and training data covers 140+ [@gemma4-model-card]
Provides separate safety and evaluation sections
Language support and training-data coverage are not language-specific safety results
Grok 4.7 model card
A coding benchmark describes tasks across five languages [@grok47-model-card]
Safety sections are organized by domain, including cyber and biological/chemical risk
A multilingual coding task is not a multilingual safety test

body.heading: Named-language testing is more informative than a combined label
paragraphs: Claude Sonnet 5.5’s system card gives the clearest named-language example in this sample. It reports harmful-request tests across 16 policy areas and names Arabic, English, French, Hindi, Korean, Mandarin Chinese, and Russian. The table describes harmless-response rates, with higher values better, but reports a combined result across the tested languages rather than an outcome for each one. This makes the tested language set and aggregate metric visible; it does not show that every relevant prompt, dialect, or real-world interaction was covered, nor does it establish results for languages outside the seven listed. [@claude-sonnet55-system-card]

Gemini 3.8 Flash reports an automated multilingual-safety result as a percentage-point change, with lower better for the metric shown, and describes a slight regression in non-English safety relative to Gemini 3.7 Flash. The card separately says the displayed development results are automated rather than human evaluation or red teaming, then describes manual red teaming by specialist teams outside model development. The distinction helps readers see two testing modes, but the combined multilingual value does not identify a language-by-language breakdown in the reviewed table. [@gemini38-flash-card]

Gemma 4’s card gives broad language coverage statements: it describes out-of-the-box support for 35-plus languages and training data covering more than 140. Those are provider disclosures about language support and corpus coverage. The card also has ethics, safety, evaluation, and limitation sections. The existence of both language claims and a safety section does not establish that safety outcomes were measured separately for each language. [@gemma4-model-card]

Grok 4.7’s card organizes safety evidence into areas such as cyber, biological and chemical capabilities, jailbreaks, general output safety, and mental health. It also reports a coding benchmark involving tasks written across five languages. That establishes a multilingual dimension for that coding benchmark, not for the safety evaluations. A language count in one capability test should not be carried over to a different risk domain without an explicit shared method. [@grok47-model-card]

body.heading: Three levels of language disclosure should stay distinct
paragraphs: The records support a practical coding scheme. First, **language availability** states where a provider says the model can be used. Second, **evaluation language coverage** says which languages were included in a specific test. Third, **language-disaggregated outcomes** show how the results differ across the tested languages. A document may provide one level and not the others. The distinction prevents a broad support claim from being mistaken for evidence of equal quality or equal safety across all users.

The sample contains one card with a named seven-language safety evaluation, one with a combined multilingual safety delta, one with broad language-support and training counts, and one with a multilingual coding task but domain-organized safety reporting. [@claude-sonnet55-system-card] [@gemini38-flash-card] [@gemma4-model-card] [@grok47-model-card] These are not four comparable test results. The test populations, task definitions, metrics, and ownership differ, and the documents are first-party. No model is ranked here.

This matters particularly for deployment in multilingual settings. A procurement team can ask whether a language appears in the relevant safety test, whether the model was tested on the intended task, how the score was calculated, and whether a local reviewer examined failure cases. If the documentation provides only a combined score or language count, the next step is a targeted pilot—not an assumption that the model behaves consistently across every language.

body.heading: Limits of the audit
paragraphs: The sample is limited to four public provider documents and the pages captured for this launch portfolio. It does not cover every model, every provider’s supplementary reports, or independent multilingual-safety research. “Not visible in the reviewed section” is not proof that a provider never tested that language. The article also does not evaluate translation quality, cultural nuance, dialect coverage, or the prevalence of harmful outputs.

A stronger follow-up study would define a shared set of safety tasks, include named language varieties, use local-language experts, publish prompts and scoring rules, and report outcomes by language with uncertainty. Until such evidence exists, the cards can show what their publishers disclose, but they do not support a general claim that safety is uniform across languages.
**Bottom line:** The four documents disclose different levels of multilingual safety evidence; language support, test coverage, and language-specific outcomes are not interchangeable.
**Why it matters:** Users need language-specific evidence when deploying models for people whose primary language is not English.

**Key takeaways:** Claude’s card names seven languages, including Hindi, in a harmful-request evaluation. Gemini reports a combined multilingual safety change but does not name every language in the displayed result. Gemma’s language-support counts are not safety measurements. Grok’s five-language coding benchmark should not be read as a five-language safety test.
**What changes:** Providers should identify tested languages and varieties, task scope, test ownership, metric, and per-language outcomes.

content.dek: A dated reference to Indian data-centre capacity should keep city rows, aggregate totals, project stages, and national projections in separate fields.

body.heading: Start with the source, date, geography, and stage
paragraphs: India data-centre capacity is often summarized with a single megawatt figure. The public records reviewed here describe several different quantities: operational capacity in selected markets, upcoming supply at different development stages, separate national capacity statements, and a future electricity-demand projection. They are not one continuous series. This reference preserves each source’s date and labels so readers can use each number without converting it into another measure. [@cw-india-dc-h1-2026] [@pib-india-dc-capacity-factsheet-2026] [@pib-data-centre-demand-2026-03-13] [@rajya-sabha-data-centre-capacity-2026-03-30]

Cushman & Wakefield’s India Data Centre H1 2026 update, published on 23 September 2026, gives operational-capacity and upcoming-supply values for seven markets. Its top-line figures are 1,789 MW operational and 3,860 MW of supply expected by 2030; the upcoming total is divided into 509 MW under construction and 3,351 MW in planning. These stages describe different points in a project’s development, and planned supply is not capacity that users can access today. Research 32 separately audits the seven displayed market rows and their arithmetic. This report uses the publisher’s top-line values only as one dated, seven-market reference. [@cw-india-dc-h1-2026]

body.heading: Keep national records separate from the market report
paragraphs: The Press Information Bureau’s factsheet entry dated 13 August 2026 says installed data-centre capacity grew from 375 MW in 2020 to about 1,575 MW “currently.” The page-entry date is known, but the capacity sentence gives no separate measurement cutoff. A separate PIB release posted 13 March 2026 says capacity was around 1,500 MW by 2025 and estimates data-centre electricity demand at 13.56 GW by 2031–32. [@pib-india-dc-capacity-factsheet-2026] [@pib-data-centre-demand-2026-03-13]

A Rajya Sabha answer dated 30 March 2026 gives the same approximate 375-to-1,500-MW-by-2025 history and describes 13.56 GW by 2031–32 as data-centre capacity. The answer later discusses electricity demand in transmission planning. [@rajya-sabha-data-centre-capacity-2026-03-30]

The PIB factsheet’s about-1,575-MW “current” figure and C&W’s 1,789-MW H1 2026 top-seven-market total cannot be reconciled from the records reviewed. The factsheet page is dated 13 August, but its capacity line gives no separate observation cutoff; C&W states an H1 2026 period and names seven markets. The sources do not provide a common facility list or calculation. The correct reporting choice is to show each number with its source and scope, not to declare one wrong or treat them as like-for-like national totals. The same caution applies to 13.56 GW: the 13 March PIB release calls it electricity demand, while the 30 March Rajya Sabha answer calls it data-centre capacity. [@pib-india-dc-capacity-factsheet-2026] [@cw-india-dc-h1-2026] [@pib-data-centre-demand-2026-03-13] [@rajya-sabha-data-centre-capacity-2026-03-30]

body.heading: What these records do not measure
paragraphs: Megawatts describe power or capacity, not annual electricity consumption. A value in MW cannot be converted directly into terawatt-hours without assumptions about operating time and utilization. It also cannot be translated into a count of GPUs: facilities differ in power allocated to IT equipment, cooling, backup, networking, and other services, while accelerator systems differ in power draw and configuration. None of the records above provides a common method for such conversions. [@cw-india-dc-h1-2026] [@pib-india-dc-capacity-factsheet-2026] [@pib-data-centre-demand-2026-03-13] [@rajya-sabha-data-centre-capacity-2026-03-30]

“Operational” is different from “under construction” and “planning.” An operational market estimate may still contain capacity that is not available to every customer, while announced or planned supply can change before it is commissioned. For a capacity reference, each entry should carry at least the reporting date, geography, stage, unit, source, and any definition the source provides. When a publisher reports an aggregate plus city rows, the table should also preserve whether the rows reproduce the headline total.

body.heading: How to update this reference
paragraphs: For each new market update, record the publication date and source, the geographic universe, operational values, and future supply broken down by project stage. Keep the publisher’s stated scope visible and link to a separate row-level audit when figures are recalculated. Do not merge a national government statement with a private-market estimate merely because both use MW, and do not substitute a recomputed value for a publisher’s total without an explicit method.

For government figures, preserve the exact wording and identify whether the statement refers to current capacity, planned capacity, electricity demand, or another quantity. A later answer that repeats the same number is not independent measurement unless it documents a separate dataset and method. The reviewed official statements do not establish that the C&W market totals and national figures use one shared definition. [@pib-india-dc-capacity-factsheet-2026] [@pib-data-centre-demand-2026-03-13] [@rajya-sabha-data-centre-capacity-2026-03-30]

This report is a dated reference, not an industry census. It does not estimate facilities outside the named markets, verify project status, or forecast which planned sites will be commissioned. Future editions should replace the snapshot only after checking the new source’s date, geographic coverage, project stages, and arithmetic. Until then, the safest use is to quote each figure with those boundaries attached.
**Bottom line:** India’s public data-centre figures describe different scopes and stages; keep private-market estimates, national statements, and demand projections separate.
**Why it matters:** Combining incompatible MW figures can produce a false picture of usable capacity or future electricity demand.

**Key takeaways:** C&W reports 1,789 MW operational and 3,860 MW upcoming across its H1 2026 update. The 509-MW construction and 3,351-MW planning categories are stages of upcoming supply, not current operational capacity. The PIB factsheet’s “current” 1,575-MW figure has no separate measurement cutoff; the March PIB release and Parliament answer use different labels for 13.56 GW. MW figures do not, without additional assumptions, establish annual energy use or GPU availability. Research 32 contains the separate arithmetic check of C&W’s seven displayed market rows.
**What changes:** Future updates should state their geographic universe, keep project stages distinct, and explain how a market estimate relates to national capacity statements.

articles.title: AIKosh catalog totals: what the public counts do—and do not—show
articles.author: Global AI News Editorial Desk

content_type_status.rationale: The completed draft was checked against the assigned editorial form.

content.dek: Two public snapshots report sharply different AIKosh catalog totals. Without stable counting rules, they show what was reported—not a measured rate of growth.

body.heading: Two dated totals are not a growth series
paragraphs: AIKosh is a public catalog of datasets, models and other resources related to artificial intelligence in India. A PIB factsheet entry dated 13 August 2026 reports more than 14,000 datasets and 331 models as of July 2026; a DD News report published 10 February 2026 gives 7,541 datasets and 273 models as of February. Those are two dated institutional statements about the catalog, not a verified time series. [@aikosh-pib-july-snapshot] [@aikosh-ddnews-february-snapshot]

It is tempting to subtract the earlier totals from the later ones and describe the difference as growth. The sources reviewed do not provide a shared counting method or say whether they count listings, unique datasets, model versions, duplicate records, withdrawn entries, or resources that remain accessible. The dates and numbers are clear; their comparability is not. This report therefore preserves each figure with its source and date and does not calculate a growth rate.

body.heading: The denominator is an editorial decision
paragraphs: “Dataset count” can refer to several different units. One page can describe a dataset, a collection can contain multiple files, and a dataset may have several versions or language variants. A catalog might also include records that are restricted, redirected, outdated, or incomplete. The published totals do not specify which of these cases are included or how duplicates are handled. These are questions for a future counting specification, not claims that any particular category is present in the reported totals.

For a useful public metric, the unit needs to be named before the count is published. Separate totals for catalog records, distinct datasets, model families, and versioned models would answer different questions. A dated count should also state how it treats duplicates, superseded records, private or restricted entries, and resources whose destination is no longer available. Without those rules, a larger number can reflect a broader definition as easily as a change in the underlying catalog.

body.heading: Catalog access and catalog scale are different questions
paragraphs: AIKosh’s Terms of Use describe datasets, models, tools and libraries as contributed resources and point users to specified licenses and end-use terms. That establishes a platform-level condition, not the permission or practical usability of every catalog item. A headline count measures neither how many resources a user can access nor how many are suitable for a specific research or deployment task. [@aikosh-terms]

The distinction matters for public infrastructure. Catalog scale can signal the breadth of material listed, while useful access also depends on findability, currentness, documentation, rights and delivery. Those properties need separate evidence. This report addresses the published totals and how they could be compared; Research 31 examines a purposive sample of five item pages and the fields visible to a prospective user. The sample is not used here to estimate catalog-wide quality or access. [@aikosh-terms]

body.heading: A reproducible method for future snapshots
paragraphs: Future catalog reports could make their totals comparable by publishing a short methods note with every snapshot. It should name the capture date, the record types included, the unit being counted, the rule for duplicates and versions, and how withdrawn or inaccessible records are treated. A stable record identifier and a public change log would let readers distinguish a new resource from a revised entry.

The calculation should preserve separate dataset and model totals instead of combining them into a single measure of “AI resources.” Where entries have versions, the report could show both the number of model families and the number of versioned records. Where the catalog has multiple visibility or access states, the count could publish those categories separately rather than implying that every listed item is equally available. These are recommendations for a transparent report, not descriptions of fields confirmed in the two count releases.

If a historical snapshot is not available, a future report should say so and avoid reconstructing a growth curve from press-release totals alone. A monthly archive of dated, machine-readable counts would make later changes auditable. It would also let researchers ask whether the catalog is expanding, becoming more accessible, or simply changing how it counts records—three different questions that a single headline total cannot answer.

body.heading: Findings, limitations, and open questions
paragraphs: The evidence reviewed supports a bounded finding: DD News reported 7,541 datasets and 273 models as of February, while a PIB factsheet entry dated 13 August reported more than 14,000 datasets and 331 models as of July. The report compared those statements and checked the platform’s general Terms of Use; it did not query an API, reconstruct historical records, or independently count the catalog. [@aikosh-pib-july-snapshot] [@aikosh-ddnews-february-snapshot] [@aikosh-terms]

The missing information is specific: what entity each source counted, whether both used the same inclusion rules, how they handled model and dataset versions, and whether the totals can be reproduced from archived catalog records. Until those points are answered, the two totals should be quoted separately with their dates and publisher attribution.

body.heading: What a useful catalog update should publish
paragraphs: For each release, publish the total by resource type, the precise unit, the counting date, the inclusion and deduplication rules, and links to an archived snapshot or reproducible query. Include a change log for renamed, versioned, withdrawn or newly added entries. Item-level fields such as license and access state remain important to users, but they should not be mistaken for the aggregate counting method. A separate field audit is linked in Research 31.
Until those definitions are available, AIKosh totals should be reported as dated statements from their publishers, not as a verified growth rate or a measure of usable public data.
**Bottom line:** The February and July AIKosh totals are dated snapshots; the public sources reviewed do not establish a comparable growth rate.
**Why it matters:** A catalog count can inform public reporting only when readers know what was counted, which records qualify, and how versions and duplicates were handled.

**Key takeaways:** The February 2026 DD News report gives 7,541 datasets and 273 models. The PIB factsheet entry dated 13 August 2026 reports more than 14,000 datasets and 331 models as of July. [@aikosh-pib-july-snapshot] Neither count passage supplies a shared unit, deduplication rule, or version policy. The comparison reviewed published statements; it did not recalculate catalog records.
**What changes:** Future snapshots should publish reproducible counting rules and archived, version-aware records so the totals can be compared over time.

**Methodology:** Compare the two dated count statements and the platform-level Terms of Use. No API query, historical catalog export, or independent item count was available; no growth rate is calculated.

articles.title: Agent evaluation field guide for enterprise pilots
articles.author: Global AI News Editorial Desk

content_type_status.rationale: The completed draft was checked against the assigned editorial form.

content.dek: Build a pilot around the workflow, tool access, failure modes, and recovery requirements—not a single benchmark score.

body.heading: Define what the pilot must prove
paragraphs: An enterprise pilot must answer a local operational question: can this agent complete defined work within its access, approval, reliability, and cost boundaries? The checklist below turns that question into a versioned evaluation plan. Published research can help teams choose measures, but acceptance criteria must reflect the workflow, its users, and the consequences of failure. [@agent-evaluation-survey-2025]

Before testing, write down the workflow, the user’s intended outcome, the tools available to the agent, the data it may access, and the actions it must not take. Convert those into a small, versioned task set. Include routine cases, edge cases, and examples likely to trigger a refusal, handoff, or approval. Preserve a set of tasks for later regression checks rather than tuning every prompt against the same examples.

headers: What it does not establish by itself

cells: Task completion
Whether the defined goal and acceptance criteria were met
Safe tool use or consistent results across new tasks
Output quality
Factuality, completeness, and policy compliance against a rubric
Reliability over repeated runs
Tool use
Correct tool, arguments, permissions, and action sequence
That the agent had only the access it needed
Reliability
Repeat runs, failure types, retries, and recovery behavior
Safety in a different environment
Safety and access
Denied actions, approvals, identity scope, and audit trail
Real-world risk outside the tested threat model
Operations
Latency, cost, escalation rate, and human review load
Long-term stability without ongoing monitoring

body.heading: Test the process, not just the final answer
paragraphs: An agent can produce a plausible final answer after using the wrong tool, making an unauthorized attempt, or receiving substantial human correction. Capture the action trace and intermediate decisions where the platform permits. Score the final result, but also inspect tool selection, arguments, permission checks, rejected actions, retries, and handoffs. A trace makes the pilot’s evidence reviewable; it does not replace task scoring or a security review.

Public benchmarks can show how researchers test tasks, but their scores should not become local acceptance thresholds by default. Compare the benchmark’s task shape, tool set, environment, scoring rules, data access, and recovery requirements with the pilot before treating it as relevant. This field guide does not adopt a benchmark score as a target: a local result is meaningful only when the task records and operating conditions are disclosed.

AgentFloor provides one bounded example: its 2026 preprint describes a deterministic 30-task benchmark organized as a six-tier capability ladder. That design illustrates one test setup; it is not a default enterprise threshold. [@agentfloor-2026]

For each metric, specify the denominator and scoring method. “Success rate” needs a definition of success. “Tool accuracy” should identify whether a correct tool call is enough or whether the action must also be authorized and useful. “Reliability” should include repeat runs and failure handling. If human reviewers score outputs, publish the rubric and the process for resolving disagreements. If an automated judge is used, compare it with a sample of human decisions instead of assuming it is unbiased.

body.heading: Include controls and recovery in the acceptance test
paragraphs: A pilot should verify that the agent has the correct identity, a limited tool set, and a clear approval path for sensitive actions. The OpenAI Agents SDK documents a flow in which a tool call can pause execution for approval and resume after a decision. Its documentation also says the application must authenticate and authorize the person approving the action. That makes approval a testable integration requirement, not a property guaranteed by adding a prompt to the agent. [@openai-agents-hitl-doc]

Auditability also needs a test. Google’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform documentation distinguishes Admin Activity, Data Access, and System Event logs; Data Access logging is disabled by default. A pilot should confirm which events are available, whether the relevant logging is enabled, and whether the organization can retrieve the records it needs. A log that exists but is unavailable to the review team does not meet an operational requirement. [@google-agent-audit-logging]

Test what happens when a tool fails, the model times out, an approval is rejected, or the run is interrupted. The agent should stop or recover in a known way, preserve enough state for review, and avoid repeating an action that may already have succeeded. Include a rollback or manual completion procedure for actions that affect customer records, money, infrastructure, or other high-impact systems.

body.heading: Set thresholds before looking at the result
paragraphs: Choose acceptance limits before the pilot starts. Possible thresholds include minimum completion rate on the defined task set, maximum unauthorized-action attempts, maximum escalation load, and required trace completeness. A pilot can also establish a baseline for human review time and operating cost. Thresholds should match business risk: a reversible draft-writing task and an irreversible production action should not share one pass/fail rule.

The test plan should state the model and checkpoint, prompts, tools, permissions, software version, dataset, evaluation period, and any human intervention. Re-run the same suite after a model update or tool change, but keep the prior result so users can see whether a change helped or introduced regressions. Benchmark scores can inform the test design, but they do not replace a local evaluation.

body.heading: Limits of this guide
paragraphs: This guide is a planning template, not evidence of product performance. OpenAI and Google documentation describes specific platform capabilities, not how a customer configured them. No benchmark establishes that a local deployment has appropriate permissions, recovery behavior, or operating cost. Those questions require a local test with the actual tools, identity, data, and approval path.
**Bottom line:** An enterprise pilot should evaluate task results, action traces, reliability, safety, permissions, and recovery as separate requirements.
**Why it matters:** A demo can succeed while hiding weak recovery, broad permissions, high human-review costs, or an incomplete audit trail.

**Key takeaways:** Define the task and boundary before choosing a benchmark. Score the trace and tool actions as well as the final response. Test repeatability, interruptions, approval rejection, and tool failure. Verify identity and audit settings in the actual deployment. Set risk-based acceptance thresholds before running the pilot.
**What changes:** Preserve a versioned evaluation suite and rerun it after model, tool, prompt, or permission changes.

articles.title: AI agent security: controls at tools, identity, and approval
articles.author: Global AI News Editorial Desk

content_type_status.rationale: The completed draft was checked against the assigned editorial form.

content.dek: Review an agent’s identity, tool permissions, approvals, runtime boundaries, and audit trail as separate controls.

body.heading: Use the register to request evidence
paragraphs: OWASP’s agent-risk guidance identifies categories such as tool misuse and identity or privilege abuse; its Agent Control Standard describes a project direction for runtime policy and observability. Neither source certifies a vendor or deployment. This register translates those topics into evidence a reviewer can request and test, rather than ranking products or prescribing a single architecture. [@owasp-agentic-top10-2025] [@owasp-acs-2026]

cells: Identity and privilege
Prefer an identity whose access matches the user or service performing the task
Credential owner, scope, expiry, delegation behavior
Tool misuse
Allow only required tools and restrict arguments or destinations where possible
Tool list, allow/deny rules, sandbox and network boundaries
High-impact action
Pause for a named, authorized reviewer when policy requires approval
Approval event, approver identity, decision binding, rejection behavior
Runtime policy
Enforce policy at a control point outside the model’s natural-language instructions
Hook or middleware configuration, deny behavior, failure mode
Audit and investigation
Record actor, action, time, target, decision, and result
Log categories, retention, access controls, and retrieval test
Recovery
Stop, resume, or roll back safely after interruption or failure
Duplicate-action protection, state integrity, recovery test

body.heading: Verify identity and permission evidence
paragraphs: Ask the owner to identify the service or user principal, credential scope and expiry, delegation behavior, and revocation process. LangSmith Fleet documentation distinguishes fixed credentials from user credentials and describes role- and attribute-based tool access; Claude Code documents allow, ask, and deny rules for tools. These are product-specific capabilities, not proof that they are enabled or correctly configured in the system under review. The audit record should include the actual configuration and a test showing that an out-of-scope request is rejected. [@langsmith-fleet-oversight] [@anthropic-claude-code-permissions]

body.heading: Confirm approval evidence
paragraphs: The OpenAI Agents SDK documents a tool call pausing for approval and resuming after a decision; the application must authenticate and authorize the approver. Reviewers should confirm that the recorded decision identifies the approver and applies to the exact operation and arguments, then inspect rejection, timeout, stale-request, and replay behavior. A product’s approval feature does not show that a deployment has connected it to the right identity or policy. [@openai-agents-hitl-doc]

body.heading: Record logging configuration and retrieval
paragraphs: Google’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform documentation distinguishes Admin Activity and System Event logs, which are always enabled, from Data Access logs, which are disabled by default. Reviewers should record which event classes are enabled, who can retrieve them, their retention period, and whether a representative tool action appears in the expected log. A logging statement in a product guide is not evidence that the organization can retrieve the records it needs. [@google-agent-audit-logging]

body.heading: Inspect the runtime enforcement path
paragraphs: Request a map of where each tool call is authorized, which operations bypass that check, and what happens if the policy hook is unavailable. Inspect a denied-action trace and confirm that high-impact operations stop rather than proceed under a fallback permission. The Agent Control Standard describes runtime hooks as a design direction; the reviewer still needs evidence that the deployed control covers the tools and side effects in scope. [@owasp-acs-2026]

body.heading: A review sequence for an agent deployment
paragraphs: Before launch, identify the agent’s service and user identities, tools, data scopes, and irreversible actions. Confirm that the minimum required privileges are used. Test approved, denied, and approval-required paths, including malformed inputs and untrusted content. Verify that logs capture the right actor and event, that sensitive data is not accidentally exposed in stored run state, and that interruptions cannot duplicate an action. Finally, document an owner and a rollback route for each high-impact workflow.

This checklist is not a certification standard and does not replace a threat model or penetration test. The cited sources include a community threat list, a project standard, and product documentation. They support control questions, but they do not prove a customer configuration is secure or show comparative product effectiveness.

body.heading: Keep an evidence packet for each workflow
paragraphs: For one high-impact workflow, record its owner, requesting principal, data involved, tool set, target resources, and the side effects the agent can create. Attach the deployed permission configuration, approval policy, logging settings, and recovery procedure. Link each control claim to an artifact from the environment under review: a vendor page can show that a feature exists, but not that it is enabled or covers this workflow.

Capture one authorized action, one denied request, one approval-required action, and one interrupted or failed run. For each, preserve the expected and observed result, the identity presented to the tool, the target and arguments, the approval decision, and a trace that a reviewer can retrieve. The failed test must stop at an enforcement point; a model saying “I can’t” does not show that a tool request was blocked. [@openai-agents-hitl-doc] [@google-agent-audit-logging]

Classify each evidence gap as a missing control, a configuration gap, an unavailable trace, or an inconclusive test. Assign an owner and a retest date, and keep failed and remediated results together. This does not certify the workflow; it makes the remaining risk specific enough for an accountable review.
Close a review item only after the retest passes and the trace can be retrieved; a configuration change without a retest leaves the evidence packet incomplete.
**Bottom line:** Secure agent deployment requires separate, testable controls for identity, tools, approvals, runtime policy, audit, and recovery.
**Why it matters:** A well-written instruction cannot compensate for an agent that has broad credentials or can execute sensitive actions without a traceable decision.

**Key takeaways:** Threat guidance helps identify risks but is not a universal compliance rule. User identity, shared credentials, tool permissions, and approval are distinct decisions. Approval workflows need application-level authentication and authorization. Logs aid investigation but do not prevent unauthorized actions. Verify behavior in the actual environment; documentation alone is not a security test.
**What changes:** Maintain a deployment control register linking each high-impact action to its identity, permission, approval, logging, and recovery requirements.

body.heading: An archive should preserve evidence, not rewrite the launch
paragraphs: Model documentation is useful only if readers can find the exact record that supports a claim. A model card, system card, and launch page may all contain evaluation information, but they are not interchangeable documents. A card can describe a model’s intended use, limitations, training or evaluation scope. A system card can provide a broader account of deployment risk and testing. A launch page may announce access and selected results without providing a standalone card. This archive keeps those formats distinct. [@gemma4-model-card] [@gemini38-flash-card] [@claude-sonnet55-system-card] [@grok47-model-card] [@openai-gpt6-sol-luna-release]

The dates above are publication dates only where the captured record shows one; the Gemma 4 card and OpenAI release page do not expose a publication date in the captured pages. The OpenAI page does show a separate 29 September update notice. These dates are not a shared standard for when a model was released or became available. A card may be published after an announcement; a product or API may arrive on a different date. Report 50 tracks those events as a timeline. This archive instead points readers back to the underlying documentation and records what kind of evidence it contains. [@gemma4-model-card] [@gemini38-flash-card] [@claude-sonnet55-system-card] [@grok47-model-card] [@openai-gpt6-sol-luna-release]

cells: Google AI for Developers — Gemma 4
Model card
No publication date visible in the captured page; captured 4 October 2026

The card contains model variants, intended-use and limitation sections, evaluation data, and parameter details. Its fields should not be compared directly with a provider’s system-card rubric. [@gemma4-model-card]
Google DeepMind — Gemini 3.8 Flash
Model card
Published 2 September 2026

The card says it may be updated as the model changes; it reports provider-run evaluations and lists known limitations, including hallucinations and occasional timeout or slowness. [@gemini38-flash-card]
Anthropic — Claude Sonnet 5.5
System card
28 September 2026
The card documents evaluation scope and limitations, including assessments it says are costly or labor-intensive; the listed results remain Anthropic’s own disclosures. [@claude-sonnet55-system-card]
xAI — Grok 4.7
Model card
21 September 2026
The card reports benchmark results and says some benchmark versions changed; comparisons across versions may therefore be invalid. [@grok47-model-card]
OpenAI — GPT-6 Sol and Luna
Release page, not a standalone model card
No publication date visible in the captured page; a 29 September 2026 update points to GPT-6.1 Sol
Keep it in a companion release index so its document type is not mistaken for a model card. Its evaluations and comparisons are OpenAI-reported. [@openai-gpt6-sol-luna-release]

body.heading: Keep the fields that make a card findable
paragraphs: An archive record should contain the provider, exact model name, document type, source URL, visible publication or update date, retrieval date, and a short description of disclosed scope. If the publisher updates the page without a clear version label, keep a dated capture and note that the record changed. This prevents a later reader from treating today’s page as proof of what was available when an earlier report was written.

The fields also need boundaries. A provider’s benchmark score should be tagged as provider-reported unless an independent evaluation is cited. A card’s limitation section is evidence of what the publisher chose to disclose; it does not prove that the list is complete. A document’s inclusion in this index is not an endorsement, a ranking, or a safety assessment. [@gemma4-model-card] [@gemini38-flash-card] [@claude-sonnet55-system-card] [@grok47-model-card]

body.heading: A compact comparison without a quality ranking
paragraphs: The five records are not a like-for-like benchmark. The Gemma 4 page identifies effective and total parameter counts separately for some variants. Gemini 3.8 Flash’s card describes its own evaluation date and its relationship to earlier model-family testing. Anthropic’s system card includes domain-specific evaluation and external testing disclosures. xAI describes both benchmark performance and a deployed-checkpoint convention. OpenAI’s Sol/Luna page presents launch information and provider-selected results, but it is not a standalone model card. These differences are useful when judging the record’s scope; they do not support a cross-provider performance ranking. [@gemma4-model-card] [@gemini38-flash-card] [@claude-sonnet55-system-card] [@grok47-model-card] [@openai-gpt6-sol-luna-release]

Readers should also avoid assuming that a card’s existence means every relevant field is present. A missing publication date is not evidence that a provider did not publish a card; it means this captured page does not expose a date that can be confidently entered. A short launch page should not be described as a missing safety card unless the provider’s documentation index has been checked. Archive language should report what the page shows, not infer the publisher’s intent.

body.heading: How to maintain the archive
paragraphs: When a provider posts a revised card, add a new version entry or a dated update record rather than overwriting the previous capture. Record the URL that was reviewed, the retrieval date, any explicit version string, and the sections changed. Link to the publisher’s current page and retain a prior snapshot when the project’s evidence policy permits it. If the page is removed or replaced, mark that status rather than silently deleting the record.

Separate cards from adjacent records: announcement, API documentation, benchmark post, system card, and third-party test should have distinct types. A source map can then point from a story to the document that actually supports each claim. Independent testing should be listed separately, with its method and model version, rather than folded into the provider’s release materials.

This snapshot contains five first-party records selected because they are relevant to September 2026 coverage. It is not a complete catalogue of all 2026 model documentation. Nor does it evaluate the models themselves. Its purpose is to give readers a stable path to the original evidence and a clear warning about what that evidence can and cannot establish.
When a story cites the archive, its reference should point to the exact document row that supports the claim, not to the index as a general endorsement of the model.
**Bottom line:** Archive primary model documents by exact name, type, date, and version; do not treat launch copy, model cards, system cards, and independent tests as equivalent.
**Why it matters:** When release pages change, the underlying evidence and its disclosed limitations can become difficult to find or mischaracterized.

**Key takeaways:** The captured set includes model cards, a system card, and a launch page; they are not the same document type. A provider’s evaluation disclosures are not independent validation. Publication, announcement, and availability dates should be stored separately. A missing date in a captured page should remain unknown, not be inferred. Keep dated records when publishers revise or replace a page.
**What changes:** A useful archive should expose stable source links, capture dates, document types, version history, and separate independent tests.

articles.author: Global AI News Editorial Desk

content.dek: A dated status table separates the EU AI Act’s staged application, official implementation guidance, and the separate EU KIDS Act proposal.

body.heading: A legal status map needs more than one start date
paragraphs: The EU AI Act is a regulation with staged application dates. The consolidated text of Article 113 gives a general application date of 2 August 2026, but it also lists provisions that applied earlier and exceptions that apply later. The European Commission’s public materials separately describe general-purpose AI (GPAI) obligations and its enforcement role. A useful status reference should identify which document supplies each date rather than reducing the whole law to a single “effective from” headline. [@eu-aiact-article-113] [@eu-gpai-obligations] [@eu-commission-enforcement-2026]

The table is a navigation aid rather than a substitute for reading the relevant articles. Article 113 is the controlling source for staged dates; the Commission’s GPAI page explains obligations for providers and distinguishes the application timetable from the Commission’s enforcement function. The Commission said its GPAI enforcement powers begin on 2 August 2026, while providers of models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 have until 2 August 2027 to comply with the relevant GPAI obligations. Those are different transitions: one concerns the Commission’s role, the other a transition for pre-existing models. [@eu-aiact-article-113] [@eu-gpai-obligations] [@eu-gpai-guidelines] [@eu-commission-enforcement-2026]

headers: Date or stage stated in official material

cells: Chapters I and II, with stated exceptions
2 February 2025; specified Article 5 provisions have a later 2 December 2026 date
A staged application date, not the start date for every obligation. [@eu-aiact-article-113]
Chapter III, Section 4; Chapters V, VII and XII; Article 78
2 August 2025; Article 101 is excepted from this stage
Apply the exact provision and exception when describing GPAI provider obligations. [@eu-aiact-article-113]
Article 101, fines for GPAI-model providers
2 August 2026 under the general application date; excluded from the 2 August 2025 stage
Keep this provision separate from the earlier GPAI obligations date. [@eu-aiact-article-113] [@eu-gpai-obligations]
Articles 102–110
