body.heading: Guidance is not the same as the regulation
paragraphs: Commission guidance, templates, and codes of practice can help organizations understand implementation expectations. They do not change the enacted text by themselves. When a report refers to a specific duty, it should link the regulation article and name the relevant guidance separately. When a page describes a code or template as voluntary, retain that label and avoid describing it as a mandatory legal obligation. [@eu-gpai-guidelines] [@eu-gpai-obligations]

This distinction is particularly important for GPAI providers. The Commission’s materials explain which provider duties apply, the timeline, and the role of the AI Office. A company announcement that it has signed a code or adopted a template is evidence of that company’s stated action; it is not by itself proof that every applicable requirement has been met. The legal question depends on the provider, model, date, and specific provision.

body.heading: The EU KIDS Act remains a proposal
paragraphs: The European Commission presented the EU KIDS Act proposal in September 2026. The proposal would address protections for children in digital environments, but the proposed text has not become an enacted regulation. A proposal can change during negotiation, and its obligations cannot be reported as current law. The Commission’s proposal document and legislative metadata establish that it is proposed; the date and legal status should be checked again before publication or reuse. [@eu-kids-act-proposal-2026]

For a side-by-side account, keep the existing AI Act in one column and the proposed KIDS Act in another. Separate the legal instrument, its status, the people or services it would cover, and the obligations described in the text. Avoid saying that the proposal “amends the AI Act” unless the official text confirms the precise legal mechanism. Do not infer a compliance deadline from a proposal’s target date.

body.heading: A practical update protocol
paragraphs: For every update to this reference, check the current consolidated regulation, the relevant Commission page, and the legislative record for any proposal discussed. Record the page or document date and the date checked. Copy dates alongside the exact article or transition they govern. If an amendment changes Article 113 or another cited provision, revise the table and state which version of the consolidated text was used.

Organizations should map these public dates to their own role and systems rather than assuming the same requirement applies to every provider, deployer, importer, or distributor. A general-purpose model provider, a deployer of a high-risk system, and an organization using a consumer-facing AI service may face different provisions. This report identifies public legal stages; it does not decide which category an individual organization falls into.

Each internal entry should also preserve the date the source was checked and the exact provision it relies on. That makes it possible to distinguish a later change in official guidance from a change in the enacted regulation, and to revisit the classification without silently rewriting the earlier assessment.

A published summary should show a “checked through” date beside each status, not only the date of the underlying law. If the current consolidated text was not reviewed, mark that limitation and recheck the status before reuse.
**Bottom line:** As of 4 October 2026, the EU AI Act is in staged application, Commission guidance is distinct from the regulation, and the EU KIDS Act is still a proposal.
**Why it matters:** Confusing a proposal, guidance document, and current legal duty can cause teams to misstate their obligations.

**Key takeaways:** Article 113 includes earlier and later dates around the general 2 August 2026 application date. GPAI obligations and Commission enforcement powers have separate transition dates. Commission guidance and codes should be labeled separately from enacted law. The EU KIDS Act proposal is not a current legal obligation. Recheck the consolidated text and proposal status before each update.
**What changes:** Maintain a dated legal-status table keyed to article, affected actor, application date, and proposal status.

articles.title: India data-centre resource evidence: energy, water, and grid limits
articles.author: Global AI News Editorial Desk

content_type_status.rationale: The draft is a reusable, source-backed evidence reference that organizes energy, water, and grid constraints rather than presenting one new empirical study. The Report label fits the synthesis and lookup purpose.

content.dek: India’s data-centre power, water, capacity, and grid claims come from different sources and evidence types. Keep each estimate attached to its attribution, date, and measurement boundary.

body.heading: Build an evidence register, not a single forecast
paragraphs: Indian data-centre reporting brings together capacity statements, secondary estimates of electricity and water use, and discussion of grid constraints. These are not one consistent measurement series. This register focuses on the India-specific evidence and preserves each source’s attribution and limitations; it is not a national meter reading or an AI-only inventory. [@ceew-india-data-centre-resource-study] [@ieefa-india-data-centre-grid-analysis]

The CEEW and IEEFA figures should not be added or treated as one measured series. The electricity share, water estimate, capacity baseline, future capacity, and projected electricity share come from different underlying reports and use different units and dates. Attribution and evidence labels are part of the record, not optional footnotes. [@ceew-india-data-centre-resource-study] [@ieefa-india-data-centre-grid-analysis]

cells: CEEW data-centre study
India, 2024
About 0.5% of national electricity and about 150 billion litres of water
CEEW cites external estimates for these figures; not direct national metering by CEEW. [@ceew-india-data-centre-resource-study]
IEEFA India analysis
India; “last year” in an article dated 6 June 2025 (2024 baseline), with forecasts to 2030
IEEFA cites 1.4 GW for the 2024 baseline, 9 GW for 2030, and a 3% electricity-use estimate for 2030
Figures are attributed to other reports and forecasts; the 3% is not measured use. [@ieefa-india-data-centre-grid-analysis]

body.heading: Separate sector growth from AI attribution
paragraphs: The same discipline is needed for India. CEEW’s report places data-centre growth in the context of power, water, land, and state policy. It says that its 2024 electricity and water figures come from external studies and that both could more than double by 2030. That is an attributed estimate and projection, not a national meter reading or a measurement of AI facilities alone. IEEFA’s article, dated 6 June 2025, uses the relative phrase “last year” for a 1.4-GW capacity baseline, which places that source’s baseline in 2024; it cites 9 GW for 2030 and points to a forecast that data centres could use around 3% of India’s electricity by then. Preserve the source’s wording alongside the inferred year when reusing the figure. These numbers describe forecasts with dependencies; they should not be presented as observed outcomes. [@ceew-india-data-centre-resource-study] [@ieefa-india-data-centre-grid-analysis]

Capacity and electricity use are related, but they are not interchangeable. A capacity value in GW describes a power level; annual consumption in TWh depends on load and operating time. A data-centre capacity forecast cannot be turned into annual energy without assumptions about utilization, facility efficiency, and what power boundary the source counts. Likewise, a water-use estimate should state whether it includes on-site cooling, indirect water associated with electricity generation, or both.

For a siting or sourcing decision, keep four evidence tracks separate: reported electricity share, water use, planned capacity, and grid access. They describe different questions, even when they concern the same sector. A value in one track does not validate the others; a national estimate cannot establish that a particular facility has a dependable connection or a measured water balance. Readers should request site-level records before applying sector claims to an operational decision.

body.heading: Grid access and resource use need their own evidence
paragraphs: The India sources also show why an energy-only headline may conceal operational constraints. IEEFA describes concentrated demand around major data-centre hubs and discusses renewable supply, storage, grid connections, and local power networks. CEEW reports stakeholder views on grid limitations and dual sourcing, where a facility can maintain a full-capacity grid connection while purchasing part of its energy through non-discom renewable routes. These arrangements may affect how grid capacity and contracted clean energy are interpreted; they do not prove that a data centre receives uninterrupted renewable electricity every hour. [@ieefa-india-data-centre-grid-analysis] [@ceew-india-data-centre-resource-study]

Water is a separate location-specific resource question. CEEW notes that water risks vary by site and that smaller facilities may rely heavily on municipal supplies. The report describes state policy provisions on water governance and cooling, but policy text does not establish actual consumption at a particular facility. A useful operational comparison would need facility-level water withdrawals, recycled water, cooling technology, local basin stress, and a consistent boundary. [@ceew-india-data-centre-resource-study]

body.heading: How to update the evidence register
paragraphs: For each new figure, retain the publisher, original data source, publication date, geography, measurement period, unit, denominator, and whether it is an observation, estimate, scenario, or forecast. Record whether AI workloads are isolated, whether the value is facility power or IT load, and whether water includes direct or indirect use. If a report repeats a number from another organization, link the original and identify the attribution.

Do not convert GW to TWh without a stated utilization assumption. Do not convert a national percentage into AI’s share without workload-level allocation. Do not interpret an announced renewable contract as proof of 24/7 carbon-free supply. Do not treat a scenario’s high endpoint as the expected outcome. Where sources disagree, preserve both values and their methods until a comparable boundary is available.

This report is an India-focused reference, not a comprehensive national inventory. It does not provide facility-level measurements, a consistent time series, or an AI-specific electricity total. The figures are dated claims and attributed estimates that retain their underlying scope.
**Bottom line:** Public data-centre energy evidence spans observed increases, estimates, scenarios, and attributed forecasts; each number needs its own source and scope.
**Why it matters:** Combining different geographies and evidence types can make an uncertain forecast appear like a measured, AI-only total.

**Key takeaways:** CEEW and IEEFA cite secondary Indian estimates and projections; they are not facility-level measurements. Capacity, electricity consumption, renewable procurement, and water use require different units and boundaries. Grid connection and water availability vary by site and cannot be inferred from a national total.
**What changes:** A useful annual update should include source provenance, native units, geography, period, evidence type, and any AI-specific allocation method.

content.dek: Estimate weight memory first, then account for context, runtime, concurrency, and task quality before selecting a local model.

body.heading: Start with the workload, not the model label
paragraphs: “Small” can describe a product family, an active-parameter count, or a model intended for edge devices. Those labels do not guarantee that the complete model will fit in a particular device’s memory. Google lists Gemma 4 variants at E2B, E4B, 12B, 31B, and 26B A4B, with different context limits and quantization options. Mistral calls one model Small 4, but its documentation lists 119 billion total parameters and 6.5 billion active parameters. A team should check the actual model record rather than assume that the name describes its hardware footprint. [@gemma4-deployment-overview] [@mistral-small4-official-doc]

cells: What model is being loaded?
Exact model, revision, total parameters, active parameters if given, modality, license
Names and active-parameter counts do not define storage requirements
Which weights will be used?
Precision, quantization format, file size, source and conversion method
Quantization can reduce weight size and alter quality
What is the target device?
GPU/accelerator model, usable memory, system RAM, power and cooling limits
Advertised memory is not all available to the model process
What context is required?
Prompt length, output length, concurrent sequences and batch size
KV cache and activations grow with runtime use
What does the workflow require?
Task set, tool calls, latency target, privacy boundary, fallback
A model that loads may still be unsuitable for the job

body.heading: Use a weight-only estimate as a first filter
paragraphs: A quick lower-bound estimate for raw weight storage is:
**Total parameters × bits per weight ÷ 8**

Using decimal gigabytes and idealized bit widths, a 31-billion-parameter model at 16-bit precision requires about 62 GB for weights alone; at 4 bits, the arithmetic gives about 15.5 GB. For Mistral Small 4’s 119 billion total parameters, the same 4-bit arithmetic gives about 59.5 GB. These calculations do not include quantization metadata, model-specific packing, runtime buffers, KV cache, activations, operating-system use, or memory fragmentation. They are screening estimates, not measured requirements. [@gemma4-deployment-overview] [@mistral-small4-official-doc] [@llama-cpp-quantization]

NVIDIA specifies 32 GB of GDDR7 memory for the GeForce RTX 5090. The simplified 31B-at-4-bit estimate is below that capacity, but this does not prove that a 31B model will fit at the requested context length or run at an acceptable rate. The 119B-at-4-bit estimate exceeds 32 GB before runtime overhead. That says only that all weights cannot fit in the card’s memory under this simple assumption; offloading, multiple accelerators, a different quantization, or a hosted endpoint change the deployment design. [@nvidia-rtx5090-spec] [@vllm-gpu-memory]

For a mixture-of-experts model, active parameters are relevant to computation but should not be substituted automatically for total weights in the storage calculation. The operator must check how the serving runtime loads or offloads experts. Mistral’s “6.5B active” figure by itself does not establish that its 119B parameter set fits in 6.5B-parameter memory. [@mistral-small4-official-doc]

body.heading: Account for context and concurrent work
paragraphs: Weights are only one component of inference memory. vLLM’s GPU memory documentation separates model weights, KV cache, activations, CUDA and framework overhead, and other allocations. It explains that KV cache use scales with sequence length and the number of sequences in a batch. Long context, long outputs, or more concurrent users can therefore exhaust memory even when the model weights load successfully. [@vllm-gpu-memory]

The published context limits also differ: the Gemma overview lists 128K for E2B and E4B and 256K for its medium variants; Mistral Small 4 lists a 256K context. A context maximum is not a guarantee that a particular GPU can serve the maximum with a chosen batch size. Local tests should set a realistic prompt and output length, then measure memory under the expected concurrency rather than testing one short prompt. [@gemma4-deployment-overview] [@mistral-small4-official-doc] [@vllm-gpu-memory]

Power and physical constraints matter too. NVIDIA lists 575 W total graphics power and 1,000 W required system power for the RTX 5090. A workstation plan should include cooling, sustained load, available connectors, and the power envelope of the whole system, not just VRAM. These are hardware specifications, not a model-specific speed result. [@nvidia-rtx5090-spec]

body.heading: Quantization needs a quality check
paragraphs: Google documents Gemma 4 in default 16-bit precision and lower-precision formats, including quantization-aware checkpoints for supported runtimes. The llama.cpp quantization guide describes conversion and quantization formats and warns that reducing precision can introduce accuracy loss, which it discusses with measures such as perplexity and Kullback–Leibler divergence. A smaller file should therefore be tested on the task, language, and output format that matter to the deployment. [@gemma4-deployment-overview] [@llama-cpp-quantization]

This report does not compare measured tokens per second across Gemma 4, Mistral Small 4, or GPUs. The reviewed sources do not provide one independent, same-hardware, same-quantization, same-context test for these exact models. Vendor performance pages, where available, should remain attributed to the provider and should not be joined to a different model’s test as if conditions matched.

body.heading: A repeatable local deployment check
paragraphs: Before committing hardware, a team can:

Pin the model revision, license, runtime, quantization format, and hardware. Confirm the complete model file size and whether all required weights are resident or offloaded. Test at the intended context length and number of concurrent sequences. Record peak GPU memory, system RAM, startup time, latency percentiles, throughput, power, and failure rate. Compare output quality and tool behavior with the unquantized or hosted baseline using a fixed task set. Repeat runs after changing runtime, quantization, batch size, or model revision. Set a fallback for out-of-memory errors, poor-quality responses, or tasks the local model cannot complete.

Keep privacy and locality claims separate from these measurements. Running a model on a local device can change where inference occurs, but it does not by itself establish that prompts, logs, updates, backups, telemetry, and connected tools remain local. Those boundaries depend on the complete application and deployment configuration.
**Bottom line:** A parameter count can screen for weight memory, but context, quantization, runtime, device limits, and task quality determine whether a deployment is practical.
**Why it matters:** A model may load on a device and still fail at production context length, concurrency, quality, or power limits.

**Key takeaways:** Read total and active parameter counts separately. Treat bit-width arithmetic as a weight-only lower bound, not a sizing guarantee. Include KV cache, activations, runtime overhead, context, and concurrency. Quantization trades memory for possible quality change and needs task-specific checks. Do not compare speed without identical models, hardware, precision, context, and workload.
**What changes:** Maintain a dated model/device matrix with exact revisions, quantization, measured memory, and reproducible workload results.

articles.title: Content provenance implementation guide for publishers
articles.author: Global AI News Editorial Desk

content_type_status.rationale: The completed draft was checked against the assigned editorial form.

content.dek: A publisher needs a signing and verification workflow, a clear status display, and a recovery plan for credentials that are absent or no longer valid.

body.heading: Treat provenance as a record, not a truth score
paragraphs: C2PA provides a technical format for recording claims about digital content and binding a manifest to an asset. The current specification reviewed for this guide is version 2.4. A valid credential can help a reader inspect a signed provenance record; it does not prove that the depicted event is factual, that every edit is disclosed, or that the asset is trustworthy for every use. [@c2pa-spec-24] [@c2pa-independent-security-study-2026] Absence of a credential is likewise not evidence that a file is fake; credentials can be absent or stripped during handling. [@c2pa-deployment-guidance-2026]

Publishers should plan the complete asset lifecycle: capture or ingest, editing, signing, export, hosting, display, verification, and preservation. If the production system strips metadata or transforms an image after signing, the manifest may no longer bind as expected. If a later edit is legitimate, the workflow should produce a new, linked record rather than silently implying that the original signature covers the altered file. [@c2pa-deployment-guidance-2026]

body.heading: Map responsibilities and signing authority
paragraphs: First identify who creates the provenance claim and whose certificate signs it. The C2PA deployment guidance distinguishes a credential that is cryptographically valid from one whose signer is trusted through the C2PA Trust List. Those statuses should not be collapsed into a generic green “authentic” badge. The user interface should explain whether a credential is present, whether its cryptographic checks passed, and whether the signer is trusted under the verifier’s current trust policy. [@c2pa-deployment-guidance-2026]

Keep signing keys under controlled access and define how certificates are issued, renewed, protected, and revoked. A newsroom should assign an accountable owner for each signing identity and limit which systems can use it. Signing all output with a shared, untracked key makes it difficult to identify the responsible production system or respond to compromise.

body.heading: Preserve the record through the editorial workflow
paragraphs: Use tools that maintain compatible manifests when cropping, color-correcting, transcoding, or exporting a new version. Maintain the relationship between the source asset and the published derivative. If the CMS resizes images, the publisher should test whether the selected pipeline preserves or re-establishes the credential after the transformation.

The official deployment guidance recommends applying credentials automatically where possible, maintaining the provenance chain through compatible tools, and making credentials visible to users. It also describes Durable Content Credentials as a layered approach that can combine embedded credentials, watermarks, and fingerprints. A watermark can preserve a signal associated with a credential if embedded information is lost; fingerprinting can attempt to match content back to a provenance record. The guidance cautions that watermarks can be defeated and fingerprint matching is probabilistic rather than exact, so publishers should document the mechanisms they use and the failure cases they handle rather than promise recovery. [@c2pa-deployment-guidance-2026]

The open-source `c2patool` can read manifest information, produce reports, and add a manifest to a file. It is useful for testing a pipeline and inspecting a sample asset, but the tool’s ability to sign or read a claim is not proof that the underlying editorial statement is true. Run the same asset through the intended publication and verification path, not only through a command-line demonstration. [@c2pa-c2patool-docs-2026]

body.heading: Verify status and handle failures carefully
paragraphs: At the point of publication and receipt, test at least four states: a valid trusted credential; a cryptographically valid credential with an untrusted signer; a credential with an invalid or mismatched binding; and an asset with no credential. The interface should state what the verifier found and offer the record for inspection. It should not replace these states with a binary “real/fake” judgment. [@c2pa-deployment-guidance-2026] [@c2pa-c2patool-docs-2026]

Security testing belongs in the workflow. The Content Authenticity Security Tool can generate malicious manifests and files for testing parser handling, including XSS and injection cases. Its documentation says the tool creates test artifacts but does not automatically determine whether an attack succeeded; teams must run the tests against their own parsers and validate the result. [@c2pa-security-test-tool-2026]

A 2026 arXiv preprint examines C2PA specification versions 2.2 through 2.4 and real-world implementations. Its authors report concerns around timestamp manipulation, certificate revocation checks, and validator consistency. These are the authors’ security findings, not proof that every signed file is compromised. They are a reason to pin the specification and validator versions, test trust and revocation behavior, and follow subsequent corrections and independent review. [@c2pa-independent-security-study-2026]

body.heading: A publisher rollout checklist
paragraphs: Inventory every system that ingests, modifies, signs, stores, or publishes an asset. Define the signer identity, certificate owner, key access, renewal, and revocation process. Pin the C2PA version, signing library, validator, and trust-list policy used in production. Test edits, resizing, compression, format conversion, and CMS delivery against a representative asset set. Display the credential’s actual status and offer a way to inspect the manifest. Test missing, invalid, untrusted, expired, or revoked credentials without labeling the underlying content as false. Use security test cases against the parser and confirm whether they succeed in the deployed environment. Retain original assets and a documented recovery path for key compromise or a validator defect.
**Bottom line:** C2PA can make provenance claims inspectable, but a publisher must implement signing, trust, editing, display, verification, and security testing as separate controls.
**Why it matters:** A credential badge that hides trust status or fails after ordinary editing can mislead users even when the underlying standard is implemented.

**Key takeaways:** A valid credential and a trusted signer are distinct statuses. Signing records a claim; it does not verify the truth of the claim. Test the entire publishing path, including CMS transformations and the reader-facing verifier. Missing credentials do not establish that content is false. Security research and tools should inform implementation-specific testing, not be generalized into a binary verdict on every C2PA asset.
**What changes:** Maintain a versioned signing/verification profile, test corpus, status-display policy, and key-compromise response plan.

body.heading: A month of releases needs a source archive
paragraphs: This timeline covers five September 2026 model announcements or documentation events from Google DeepMind, xAI, OpenAI, and Anthropic. It is a dated snapshot checked through 4 October 2026, not a complete list of every model release. The archive separates the announcement, model or system card, and third-party availability dates so that a later report can tell what changed and when. [@google-gemini-38-audio-card] [@xai-grok47-release] [@openai-gpt6-sol-luna-2026] [@anthropic-sonnet55-system-card] [@openai-gpt61-sol-release]

The Google record is specifically about Gemini 3.8 Audio cards, not a new general-purpose text model. The card describes four audio variants and its stated limitations. The timeline therefore labels it a documentation and availability record and does not claim an independent benchmark. [@google-gemini-38-audio-card] [@techtarget-gemini-38-live-2026]

The Grok entry shows why a provider release and third-party distribution should be separate. xAI’s release and card are dated 21 September. AWS’s Bedrock page says the model is available, but the captured page does not show when it was posted, so this timeline does not assign the AWS event a date. body.heading: How to maintain the timeline
paragraphs: For each entry, preserve the original URL, publisher, publication date, document type, and retrieval date. Keep announcement date separate from card publication and API or hosting availability. If a source says “available now” without a separate dated record, quote that wording with the source date rather than inventing a platform date. Add later availability events as new rows so they do not overwrite the model’s original launch record.

Treat each row as an event tied to one exact model name, not as a permanent summary of the product. A single model can have a provider announcement, a card publication, an API listing, a consumer-product rollout, and a third-party hosting record. Store the event type and date as the source states it. If the page gives only a publication date and says “available now,” keep that wording rather than converting it into a precise access date. This lets a reader sort the timeline by what changed without conflating launch, documentation and distribution.

Attach evidence to the claim it supports. A provider release can establish the announcement and its own price or availability statements; a model or system card can establish the developer’s disclosed evaluation scope and limitations; a cloud record can establish a distribution route. A news report may independently confirm that an announcement occurred without independently testing the model. Benchmark results should link to the evaluation record that reports the task, conditions and metric, and be labeled as provider-reported or independently measured. Do not let a source that confirms a date appear to validate a performance claim in the same row.

When a page changes, preserve the URL, retrieval timestamp, any explicit version label, and the sections that changed. Keep the earlier capture and add an update event instead of overwriting it. If a date, test condition or platform surface is absent, mark it “not stated in the source reviewed”; absence from one captured page is not proof that the event did not happen. If a page is removed or replaced, record that status and retain the prior source reference where the evidence policy allows.

This structure makes the archive useful during a later story update. A writer can filter for announcement, evaluation, price or hosting evidence, check whether an independent test exists, and follow the exact record behind each statement. Repeated coverage of one vendor result should remain one performance source plus secondary reporting, not a count of independent confirmations. The timeline does not rank models or determine product quality; it helps keep chronology and evidence status auditable.

This timeline does not rank the models, validate vendor benchmark claims, or infer product access from a news headline. Its job is to help readers locate the first-party record and determine whether a later article is about an announcement, evaluation document, or distribution change.
**Bottom line:** September’s model records include announcements, cards, and later platform availability; their dates should not be collapsed into one release timestamp.
**Why it matters:** A model can be announced before its documentation or third-party hosting is available, and those records support different claims.

**Key takeaways:** Gemini 3.8 Audio’s September event is a model-card publication. AWS’s Bedrock page provides a separate Grok 4.7 availability record, but its captured copy does not state a date. OpenAI’s launch pages are not treated as model cards in this archive. Anthropic’s provider evaluation claims remain attributed, even when reporting confirms the launch date. Hosting records corroborate distribution, not model quality.
**What changes:** Append a new dated event whenever a model card, API, product surface, or hosting platform becomes available.

articles.title: GPT-6 Sol or Luna? Compare the published roles
articles.author: Global AI News Editorial Desk

content_type_status.rationale: The completed draft was checked against the assigned editorial form.

content.dek: OpenAI positions Sol for harder work and Luna for lower-cost use, but its own published prices and evaluations do not establish which model fits a specific workflow.

body.heading: Compare the jobs the provider describes
paragraphs: OpenAI presents GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna as two points on its cost-and-capability range. The launch page describes Sol as suited to difficult work tasks, while Luna is positioned as a faster, lower-cost option for routine and high-volume work. These are the provider’s intended roles, not independently verified quality categories. The useful choice is therefore not “which is smarter?” based on the names, but “which should a team test first for this workload?” [@openai-gpt6-sol-luna-2026]

The prices are published per million tokens. They do not directly predict a workflow bill: output volume, prompt caching, reasoning effort, retries, tool use, and application-level orchestration can change total cost. A team should calculate its own cost per completed task using the same input data and success criteria rather than selecting by per-token price alone. [@openai-gpt6-sol-luna-2026]

body.heading: Keep vendor evaluations in their lane
paragraphs: OpenAI reports results on AutomationBench, a business-workflow evaluation, and compares models at specified reasoning-effort settings. Those numbers are useful as a description of what the company tested. They are not an independent comparison: the provider controls the model versions, runs, and reported analysis in the release page. Reuters corroborates the release and describes the commercial positioning, but its launch coverage is not a separate model benchmark. [@openai-gpt6-sol-luna-2026] [@reuters-gpt6-sol-luna-2026]

Even a same-benchmark comparison can mislead if effort settings, fallbacks, task coverage, or accounting differ. The release page itself notes that one comparison’s reported cost omits the price of a fallback model used on some tasks. That is a concrete reason to look for the cost boundary and fallback assumptions beside any score. A lower cost for a benchmark run does not prove lower cost for a production workflow with different tools, retries, or output lengths. [@openai-gpt6-sol-luna-2026]

There is also a small arithmetic issue worth preserving. The page describes the new prices as a 50% reduction from GPT-5.6 promotional prices. Its table shows Luna output moving from $1.20 to $0.50 per million tokens, which is a 58.3% reduction by direct calculation, not 50%. The page does not explain this difference. A report should quote the displayed prices and label the headline as OpenAI’s description rather than silently choosing one percentage. The Sol output values ($20 to $10) do equal 50%. [@openai-gpt6-sol-luna-2026]

body.heading: Choose a first test, then measure your own workload
paragraphs: Sol is the more natural first candidate when the task involves complex, multi-step work and a higher failure cost, if the budget supports testing it. Luna is a reasonable first candidate for repetitive or high-volume work where its published price difference may matter. Neither recommendation guarantees task quality; both should be evaluated against the same locally defined examples and acceptance rules.
A useful comparison run should:

Pin the model names and API revisions, prompts, tools, and application code. Use a held-out task set that reflects the intended workflow, including failure and handoff cases. Record reasoning-effort settings and any fallback model; do not combine results from unlike settings. Report completion rate, factual or procedural errors, human review time, retries, and total cost per accepted task. Repeat runs where outputs are stochastic and disclose the number of trials. Keep latency and quality separate; a lower time or price does not show that a task was completed correctly.

The released pages do not provide a same-conditions independent test of Sol versus Luna on a shared user-defined task set. This comparison therefore stops at published role, list price, and evidence type. It does not infer that Sol is universally better for complex work, that Luna is universally fast enough, or that the vendor’s benchmark results transfer to every application.

A useful cost sheet should separately record uncached input, cached input, and output for each completed case. Multiply each by its published rate, then include retries, fallbacks, and tool or application costs before dividing by tasks accepted under the same quality rule. Otherwise a cheap failed attempt can look less expensive than an accepted answer. This calculation does not assume which model wins; it makes the break-even visible from the team’s own runs. [@openai-gpt6-sol-luna-2026]
Report the cost separately by task family; one average can conceal where extra retries erase a price advantage or where a more capable model is unnecessary.
**Bottom line:** Sol and Luna have sharply different listed token prices and provider-described roles, but workload performance must be tested locally.
**Why it matters:** A model choice based only on a product label or per-token price can increase review effort or total cost if the selected model needs more retries.

**Key takeaways:** Treat “difficult work” and “routine work” as provider positioning, not independent findings. The published per-token rates differ by 20 times for both input and output. OpenAI’s benchmark evidence is first-party; Reuters coverage confirms the launch, not model quality. Preserve the unexplained mismatch between the “50%” headline and the Luna output table values. Run a shared, representative task set and compare total accepted-task cost.
**What changes:** Recheck the release page, model identifiers, prices, and evaluation conditions before publication or procurement.

articles.title: SWE-bench Verified versus Terminal-Bench: what coding-agent scores measure
articles.author: Global AI News Editorial Desk

content_type_status.rationale: The completed draft was checked against the assigned editorial form.

content.dek: One benchmark asks an agent to fix a real repository issue; the other asks it to complete a broader command-line task. Their scores answer different questions.

body.heading: The benchmark name is not the task
paragraphs: “Coding-agent score” can refer to very different work. SWE-bench Verified is a human-validated subset of 500 software issues drawn from real GitHub repositories. Terminal-Bench 2.0 is a set of 89 containerized command-line tasks, each with a defined environment and verification tests. One centers on issue resolution in a codebase; the other deliberately spans longer, realistic terminal workflows. Their pass rates should not be placed in one leaderboard as if they measured the same capability. [@swebench-verified-methods] [@terminal-bench-2026-paper]

SWE-bench Verified’s selection process addresses known dataset-quality concerns by having humans inspect whether issue descriptions are clear, whether tests are appropriate, and whether the task can be solved. That makes the 500-item set more curated than the original pool; it does not turn the set into a representative sample of all software engineering. Results still depend on the agent scaffold, model version, repository environment, time and token budgets, and exact evaluation harness. [@swebench-verified-methods]

Terminal-Bench 2.0’s task packaging makes a different tradeoff. The paper describes each task as an instruction, a container image, tests, and a human-written solution. Its curated environments support repeatable setup, but the authors also discuss residual non-determinism from hardware differences, external services, and infrastructure reliability. The benchmark authors emphasize manual verification because it is difficult to ensure a task is both solvable and resistant to shortcuts. [@terminal-bench-2026-paper]

body.heading: What a passing score does—and does not—mean
paragraphs: A pass means that a run met that benchmark’s grader under that benchmark’s conditions. On SWE-bench Verified, it is evidence about resolving selected repository issues with the chosen harness. On Terminal-Bench, it is evidence about completing selected terminal tasks in the specified environments. Neither score alone establishes that an agent is safe to run against production systems, handles every repository, understands user intent, or recovers reliably after tool failures.

The distinction matters for procurement. A team maintaining large software repositories may find the issue-repair task family more relevant, while a team that expects agents to install dependencies, configure services, or operate command-line tools may value terminal tasks. Even then, local acceptance testing is necessary: internal repositories, build systems, permissions, and recovery procedures may not resemble benchmark environments.

body.heading: A disciplined way to compare published results
paragraphs: Before comparing numbers, record:

Exact benchmark name and release, including dataset revision and task subset. Model version and agent scaffold, not just the model family. Tool permissions, network access, container limits, and allowed retries. Token, wall-clock, and monetary budgets. Grader version, hidden-test policy, and any human intervention. Whether the score uses one attempt or repeated trials.

Do not calculate a “winner” from a score in one paper and a score in another unless the benchmark, harness, and conditions match. A paper may also use a version of SWE-bench or Terminal-Bench with a different agent scaffold or task subset. Cite the method and evaluation date with the score, and treat version changes as possible breaks in comparability. [@swebench-verified-methods] [@terminal-bench-2026-paper]

Task count describes the size of a test set, not by itself its uncertainty or external validity. The 500 repository issues and 89 terminal tasks cover different work; the larger count is not automatically more representative, and the smaller count is not automatically less reliable. Check whether the source reports per-task outcomes, repeated runs, or a measure of run-to-run variation. If it publishes only an aggregate, treat a narrow score margin as unresolved rather than a dependable ordering. Use the benchmark to select local tasks, then rerun with the repository, tools, budget, and acceptance rule that matter to the deployment. [@swebench-verified-methods] [@terminal-bench-2026-paper]

Even a strong benchmark result should prioritize local evaluation, not replace code review, security review, or clear human ownership of production changes. The benchmark’s grader determines a pass under its rules; it does not decide whether the resulting software is ready to deploy.

body.heading: Use both as evidence, not as certification
paragraphs: The benchmarks are complementary examples of coding-agent work rather than competitors for one universal title. A high score on the first does not imply high performance on the second, and a low score may reflect model limits, agent orchestration, tooling, or environment fit. For a deployment decision, select tasks that represent the actual job, then add safety, authorization, review, and recovery criteria that these benchmark scores do not provide.
**Bottom line:** SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench test different task families, environments, and graders; report their scores separately.
**Why it matters:** Treating benchmark results as interchangeable can lead a team to select an agent for work the benchmark never tested.

**Key takeaways:** SWE-bench Verified covers 500 human-validated GitHub issue instances. Terminal-Bench 2.0 covers 89 curated command-line tasks in containerized environments. Their graders and task families differ, so raw scores should not be pooled. Both remain bounded tests and do not certify safe production use. Pin the benchmark, agent, harness, budgets, and grader before interpreting a result.
**What changes:** Maintain a task-specific benchmark sheet and re-run the relevant suite after a model, scaffold, or environment change.

content.dek: Compare the serving arrangement, terms, and operator workload—not the model names as if they were a controlled quality test.

body.heading: Compare access models before capability claims
paragraphs: Gemini 3.8 Flash is presented through a provider-operated API and downstream services. Gemma 4 and Mistral Small 4 are described as open-weight models that can be run through compatible software, subject to each model’s terms and implementation requirements. These choices give a team different operating responsibilities; they do not form a like-for-like quality test. [@gemini38-flash-card] [@gemma4-model-card-2026] [@mistral-small4-card-2026]

The Gemini 3.8 Flash card says the model accepts text, images, audio, and video, lists a context window up to one million tokens, and points users to API and cloud terms. It does not specify a user-managed hardware footprint. Gemma 4’s card describes open weights and model sizes; Google’s documentation lists different precision and quantization options. Mistral’s card gives total and active parameter counts and a 256K context, but the parameter label does not tell an operator which runtime, quantization, or device will work best. [@gemini38-flash-card] [@gemma4-model-card-2026] [@gemma4-overview-2026] [@mistral-small4-card-2026]

body.heading: “Open weights” shifts work; it does not remove it
paragraphs: With an open-weight deployment, the team can select the runtime, quantization, hardware, network boundary, update process, and logging. That flexibility comes with responsibility for installation, patching, performance monitoring, backup, capacity, access control, and incident response. An open license is permission to use or adapt under stated terms; it does not promise a model is accurate, safe for a specific task, or inexpensive to operate.

Mistral Small 4 is an instructive naming example. Its model card lists 119 billion total parameters and 6.5 billion active parameters. These counts distinguish the full model from the parameters activated in a given computation; the 6.5B figure is not a standalone storage or memory estimate for a local runtime. Teams should size from the exact artifact, precision, context, and runtime rather than infer hardware fit from the word “Small” or the active-parameter count. [@mistral-small4-card-2026]

body.heading: A hosted API also has multiple terms layers
paragraphs: The Gemini API Additional Terms effective 23 March 2026 distinguish unpaid from paid services. For unpaid services, Google may use prompts and responses to provide, improve, and develop products, and human reviewers may read and process API input and output; the terms say not to submit sensitive, confidential, or personal information. The terms also state that the paid-services data-use rules apply to all services, including those offered free, for users in the European Economic Area, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom. For paid services, prompts and responses are not used to improve products, while logs are kept for a limited period for prohibited-use enforcement, service safety and security, and required legal or regulatory disclosures. This comparison is specific to those Gemini API service terms and should not be generalized to other Google products, other providers, or every deployment route. [@gemini-api-terms-2026]

Before procurement, compare the exact service tier, endpoint, license, model revision, region, logging, support, and data-processing terms. A model can be open-weight but still be consumed through a hosted API with its own data contract. Conversely, a hosted model offered through a cloud platform may inherit that platform’s security and billing controls without giving the customer control of model weights.

body.heading: A practical selection sequence
paragraphs: Define the task set and quality threshold; do not use release-page benchmarks as a substitute. Decide whether the team needs weight access, offline operation, or a provider-managed API. Check license and service terms separately. Estimate hardware from total weight size, context, runtime overhead, and concurrency. Include engineering, power, patching, support, and failure-recovery costs. Test a hosted endpoint and a self-hosted candidate with the same held-out tasks if both are plausible. Document which prompts, files, logs, and tool calls cross the boundary in each design.

A total-cost comparison should use the same accepted-work target and request volume. For each route, estimate inference charges, then add the operator time for setup, updates, capacity monitoring, incidents, and recovery; include hardware and unused capacity for self-hosting, and API pricing and terms for a hosted service. A per-token quote and downloadable weights are not equivalent to a cost-free option. State assumptions about concurrency, context, and retries, and show how the estimate changes when utilization changes. This is a budgeting method, not a market-price claim. It also makes the decision order explicit: reject routes that fail a required data boundary before optimizing cost.

For a hosted route, record the model revision and endpoint behavior; for a self-hosted route, retain the artifact identifier, quantization, and runtime. Treat a revision as a new candidate, rerun the evaluation, and update the rollback plan rather than assuming the original result still applies.
Name the team responsible for capacity, updates, and incident recovery for each route; a route with no operating owner is not a complete deployment option.
**Bottom line:** Gemini’s hosted API and the Gemma/Mistral open-weight routes differ in control and operating work; these records do not establish a model-quality winner.
**Why it matters:** A team can choose a model that meets a license or deployment need yet still miss hardware, data-handling, or maintenance requirements.

**Key takeaways:** Compare access and responsibilities separately from model capability. Read the exact license and service terms for the chosen artifact and endpoint. Total parameters, context, and runtime requirements matter more than product labels. Unpaid and paid Gemini API terms differ; do not generalize one tier’s handling to every service. Use a shared task set for quality and cost comparisons.
**What changes:** Recheck model artifacts, license language, API terms, supported contexts, and runtimes before selecting a deployment route.

articles.title: Local, private-cloud, or hosted API for sensitive workflows?
articles.author: Global AI News Editorial Desk

content_type_status.rationale: The completed draft was checked against the assigned editorial form.

content.dek: “Local” and “hosted” are not privacy guarantees; map where prompts, files, logs, tools, and backups actually go.

body.heading: Pick a data boundary, not a label
paragraphs: A private workflow may contain personal, customer, commercial, legal, or internal material. Three common architectures move that material differently: inference on a device or organization-managed server; a model endpoint hosted in a private cloud environment; or a provider-operated API. The right choice depends on data flow, access controls, service terms, operational capacity, and the model quality needed for the task. A local model is not automatically private if the application sends prompts or telemetry elsewhere, and a hosted API is not automatically unsuitable if its terms and controls meet the organization’s requirements. [@nist-genai-profile] [@gemini-api-terms-2026]

cells: Local / organization-run
User or organization
Is the model and all supporting code local? Are logs, updates, retrieval, and tools also local?
More control, but hardware and operations are the team’s responsibility
Private-cloud deployment
Cloud or platform provider under an organization’s configuration
What region, tenant boundary, access roles, encryption, logs, backups, and subprocessors apply?
More scalable operations, but contractual and platform boundaries still matter
Provider API
Model provider or platform
Which service tier applies? What are retention, human review, training, logging, region, and deletion terms?
Less infrastructure work, but the prompt leaves the organization’s runtime

body.heading: What the terms can and cannot answer
paragraphs: Google’s Gemini API Additional Terms illustrate why “hosted” is too broad a category. For unpaid services, Google may use prompts and responses to improve products and human reviewers may process API input and output; the terms say not to submit sensitive, confidential, or personal information. For users in the European Economic Area, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom, the paid-services data-use terms apply to all services, including those offered free. For paid services, prompts and responses are not used to improve products, although limited-period logging may occur for prohibited-use enforcement, service safety and security, and required legal or regulatory disclosures. This is a concrete example, not a universal statement about every Gemini service or every provider. [@gemini-api-terms-2026]

The NIST Generative AI Profile offers a risk-management structure rather than a data-processing contract. Its functions encourage organizations to govern, map, measure, and manage risks, including those involving third-party resources. It does not tell a team what a particular endpoint retains or whether its terms satisfy a particular legal obligation. Those answers require the current service terms, product configuration, and the organization’s own legal and security review. [@nist-genai-profile]

body.heading: Map the complete workflow
paragraphs: For each architecture, draw the full path for a representative task:

User prompt and uploaded files. Retrieval system, browser, or document store. Model endpoint and any fallback model. Tool calls to email, code, CRM, or other systems. Application logs, observability, and human-review systems. Backups, support exports, crash reports, and deletion requests.

Then identify the controller and retention rule at each step. A local model may be paired with a remote search tool, cloud-hosted vector database, or telemetry service. A private-cloud deployment can still involve managed services and external support. A provider API may offer documented retention controls but still require approval for the data category. The diagram should describe actual network routes and configuration, not just the hosting label. [@nist-genai-profile]

body.heading: Decide with a risk-weighted matrix
paragraphs: If a workflow cannot tolerate the prompt leaving a controlled device or network, a local or organization-run architecture may be the starting point—but only after verifying the whole application’s outbound behavior. If the organization needs centralized access controls, managed infrastructure, and a contracted data boundary, a private-cloud deployment may fit, provided configuration and terms are reviewed. If a provider API offers a suitable data-processing agreement, retention policy, region, and access controls, it may reduce operations work; the team must still test those conditions.

Quality, latency, and price are separate questions. A smaller local model may require more human review or fail tasks that a hosted model handles; a hosted endpoint may have network delays or rate limits. This comparison does not measure those outcomes. Report 48 gives a hardware-planning method; this article focuses on the data boundary and governance decision.

Before approval, record the data classes allowed, the endpoint and service tier, model version, geographic route, logging defaults, retention and deletion behavior, human review, connected tools, and incident contact. Recheck these fields after a provider changes its terms or the organization changes a model, application, or endpoint.

Separate veto conditions from preferences in the risk matrix. If a data class is not permitted to leave a controlled network, external processing is a hard exclusion, not a score that can be outweighed by lower latency. After admissible routes are identified, compare quality, operating support, cost, and review load. If no option meets both the data boundary and task threshold, defer the automation or keep the human process rather than hiding the unresolved risk in an average score. Record who may approve exceptions and what changes trigger a new review.
Tie each approval to the specific endpoint, data class, and fallback route; changing a region or logging service creates a new data flow to assess, not an exception to assume.
Reassess when retrieval, tool, or telemetry integrations change, not only when the model provider changes.
**Bottom line:** Choose an inference route only after tracing every data path and matching the actual terms and controls to the workflow’s risk.
**Why it matters:** Sensitive data can leave through a retrieval, logging, or tool integration even when the model itself runs locally.

**Key takeaways:** “Local,” “private cloud,” and “hosted API” describe deployment shapes, not complete privacy outcomes. Map prompts, files, retrieval, tools, logs, backups, and telemetry. Read terms for the exact product, tier, endpoint, and region. NIST AI 600-1 supports risk management but does not replace a contract or legal review. Keep model quality, privacy, latency, and cost as separate comparison axes.
**What changes:** Maintain a data-flow diagram and approved endpoint register for every sensitive AI workflow.

articles.title: Task success, pass^k, or action traces? Choosing agent evaluation measures
articles.author: Global AI News Editorial Desk

content_type_status.rationale: The completed draft was checked against the assigned editorial form.

content.dek: A one-run score, a repeated-run reliability measure, and a tool-action trace answer different questions about an agent.

body.heading: Three measures, three questions
paragraphs: Agent evaluations often compress a complex run into a percentage. Before comparing results, identify what the percentage counts. A task-success score asks how often a run met its acceptance condition. τ-bench’s pass^k estimates how often all k independently sampled trials for a task succeed; its paper distinguishes this from pass@k, which in code-generation literature counts whether at least one of k trials succeeds. A trajectory or action trace records what the agent did along the way—tools, arguments, approvals, and recovery steps. No one measure covers all three concerns. [@agent-evaluation-survey-2025] [@tau-bench-2024]

τ-bench defines pass^k as the probability that all k independent trials for a task succeed, averaged across tasks. It uses tool-agent-user interactions in domains such as retail and airline service, where a final database state and required response content can be checked against an annotated outcome. This makes repeated success useful for studying consistency under that benchmark’s simulated environment. It does not establish reliability in an enterprise system with different tools, users, or policies. [@tau-bench-2024]

cells: One-run task success
Did this attempt meet the grader?
Capability snapshot on a defined task set
A single success may hide inconsistency
Repeated-run pass^k
Did every one of k trials for a task succeed?
Reliability-sensitive workflows
Depends on trial design, independence, and task mix
Action trace / trajectory review
What tools, decisions, and recoveries led to the result?
Safety, policy compliance, and debugging
Requires a rubric; a longer trace is not automatically better

body.heading: Why one-run success is not reliability
paragraphs: If a system succeeds on a task in one run, the single-run score records that attempt as a success. It does not say whether the next run will follow the same path. In a simplified illustration—not an observed benchmark result—an agent with an 80% independent per-run success probability would have a 32.8% probability of succeeding on all five runs (0.8⁵). That gap shows why repeated success is a stricter requirement for workflows where every attempt must be correct.

The independence assumption is important. Real runs may share prompts, model versions, tools, outages, or systematic errors, so results are not necessarily independent draws. An evaluator should publish k, the number of trials per task, how tasks were selected, and whether failures share a likely cause. Report the per-task or distributional information when possible rather than presenting one average without a denominator. [@tau-bench-2024]

body.heading: What traces add
paragraphs: A successful final state can conceal an unsafe or expensive path. The agent may have tried a prohibited tool, exposed data, made a duplicate write, or relied on an unrecorded human correction. A trace review asks whether the sequence was authorized and recoverable, not only whether the output passed. The evaluation survey separates objectives such as task completion, reliability, capability, and safety from the processes and metrics used to measure them. This supports treating outcome and process evidence as related but distinct. [@agent-evaluation-survey-2025]

Traces also have limits. There is no universal “trajectory quality” score. A rubric must define which actions are required or forbidden, how tool arguments are assessed, what counts as a justified retry, and whether a human handoff is a failure or the correct safe outcome. Collect only the information needed for evaluation and protect traces that contain sensitive prompts or data.

Terminal-Bench 2.0 illustrates a benchmark built around outcome verification: each task has a containerized environment and tests that inspect final state. Its authors also discuss residual non-determinism and the work needed to manually validate tasks. An outcome grader is useful for checking task completion, but it should be paired with a trace review when deployment decisions depend on permissions, cost, or recovery. [@terminal-bench-2026-paper]

body.heading: Use a metric set that matches the risk
paragraphs: For a reversible drafting task, a one-run completion rate plus reviewer quality score may be adequate for an initial comparison. For a workflow that sends customer messages or changes records, repeated-run success, unauthorized-action attempts, duplicate-write checks, and audit-trace review matter more. For a long-horizon agent, record interruptions, handoffs, retries, partial completion, and recovery cost as well as final success.

Do not compare a one-run success rate from one benchmark to pass^k from another, or turn a trace rubric into a model ranking unless the task, agent, and grader are controlled. Choose the metric before the run, state the denominator and threshold, and report the environment and number of trials.

A decision report should separate “can perform” from “is safe to delegate.” Set an outcome threshold and any repeated-run requirement in advance, plus a distinct criterion for disallowed actions. Review traces when a successful final state could conceal an unsafe intermediate step. If one dimension misses its threshold, do not average it away with a strong result on another. Recording the decision rule before a run prevents the team from changing its weighting after seeing the scores.
A scorecard should keep severe policy violations visible as counts, not bury them inside aggregate task success or an average quality score.
**Bottom line:** One-run success measures a result, pass^k measures repeated consistency, and action traces expose the path; use more than one when risk requires it.
**Why it matters:** An agent can occasionally succeed while remaining inconsistent or taking an unsafe route.

**Key takeaways:** Define what “success” means and state the denominator. Use repeated runs when consistency matters. Review traces for authorization, tool behavior, retries, and recovery. Treat pass^k’s independence assumption and task mix as part of the result. No metric or benchmark alone certifies a production agent.
**What changes:** Report one-run outcome, repeated-run reliability, and process evidence as separate fields in evaluation records.

articles.title: Read-only, approval-gated, or unrestricted agent tools?
articles.author: Global AI News Editorial Desk

content_type_status.rationale: The completed draft was checked against the assigned editorial form.

content.dek: Match an agent’s authority to the consequences of its actions; “human approval” only helps when the approval is bound to the right person and operation.

body.heading: Compare authority profiles, not vendor labels
paragraphs: An agent tool can inspect information, make a change after approval, or execute changes automatically. These are useful authority profiles for an operator to compare, but they are not standardized across products. “Read-only” should mean the connected service cannot be changed by the agent, not simply that a prompt told the model not to write. Approval-gated access means a request pauses for an authorized decision before the side effect. Unrestricted access means the tool can act without that per-action gate, subject to its configured permissions. [@owasp-agentic-top10-2025] [@anthropic-claude-code-permissions] [@openai-agents-hitl-doc]

OWASP’s agentic-application risk list includes tool misuse and identity or privilege abuse. Those risks apply even when the final answer appears reasonable: an agent may use a tool against a broader target, pass an unsafe argument, or act with a service identity that has more authority than the user. A permission mode should therefore be selected from the effect of the tool call, not from a model’s self-reported confidence. [@owasp-agentic-top10-2025]

cells: Read-only
Search, summarize, or draft from source systems
Confidential information can still be exposed or misrepresented
Confirm no write method or side-effecting endpoint is reachable
Approval-gated
Send, publish, purchase, delete, or modify records
A weak or misbound approval can authorize the wrong action
Verify approver identity, exact tool and arguments, rejection path, expiry, and audit record
Unrestricted / automatic
Low-impact, reversible, high-volume actions with narrow scope
Prompt injection, tool misuse, or credential abuse can cause direct changes
Bound permissions, targets, volume, idempotency, monitoring, and rollback

body.heading: Read-only reduces side effects, not every risk
paragraphs: A read-only design can be a good first stage for research, triage, or internal search, especially when the data is sensitive or the agent is new. It reduces the chance that an agent will change a record or send a message. It does not prevent the agent from disclosing retrieved data in its response, logging sensitive content, or passing it to another enabled tool. Teams must still limit which records can be read and decide where prompts and traces are stored.

“Read-only” also needs to be checked at the integration layer. A tool that is labelled as search might trigger a remote query, download a document, or write a cache. Review the underlying API methods and permissions. Test the agent with a prompt that asks it to modify or expose data, then inspect server-side authorization and logs rather than relying on the natural-language refusal.

body.heading: Approval gates need a security contract
paragraphs: An approval button is not a control unless the application authenticates the reviewer and binds the choice to a specific request. OpenAI’s Agents SDK documentation describes an interruption and resume flow for approval-required tool calls; it also leaves authentication and authorization of the approver to the application. The product feature therefore does not by itself prove that a company’s approval process is secure. [@openai-agents-hitl-doc]

Before enabling writes, verify that the approval view contains the action, target, and arguments; that a rejection cannot be mistaken for approval; that stale requests expire; and that the execution resumes with the same approved arguments. Record who decided and what actually executed. If the underlying state changes between review and execution, require a fresh approval or revalidate the action.

Approval gates introduce latency and reviewer workload. They are appropriate where human judgment is valuable, not as a universal wrapper around every tool. If every low-risk action asks for confirmation, users may approve reflexively. If a destructive operation bypasses review, the gate is too narrow. Define thresholds by reversibility, impact, financial exposure, data sensitivity, and external visibility.

body.heading: Automatic action requires smaller boundaries
paragraphs: Unrestricted action can be justified for a narrow, well-tested, reversible task. It should not mean that the agent receives broad credentials or can choose arbitrary destinations. Restrict the service identity, tool set, query scope, and operation volume. Use idempotency or duplicate-action checks for writes, and provide a stop and rollback route where possible.

Anthropic’s Claude Code documentation provides a product-specific example of allow, ask, and deny rules, with deny evaluated ahead of ask and allow. This demonstrates that different tools can have explicit policy precedence, but it does not establish that all agent frameworks implement the same rules or that those settings are correctly configured in a customer deployment. [@anthropic-claude-code-permissions]

body.heading: A decision sequence
paragraphs: List the tools and their possible side effects. Classify each action by impact, reversibility, data sensitivity, and external audience. Start with read-only access where it can meet the task. Add approval for specific high-impact actions, and verify the approver’s identity and decision binding. Allow automatic writes only when scope is narrow and failure is detectable and recoverable. Test denied, malformed, duplicate, stale, and interrupted actions in the actual environment.

The three profiles can coexist in one workflow: read-only discovery, approval-gated execution, and a narrow automatic post-action check. A single “autonomy level” for the whole agent can obscure which tool can actually change what.
**Bottom line:** Use the least authority that can complete the task, and validate each side-effecting tool at the integration boundary.
**Why it matters:** An agent’s permissions determine what a mistaken or manipulated action can do, regardless of the quality of its final response.

**Key takeaways:** Read-only access still carries confidentiality and data-flow risks. Approval must be authenticated and tied to the exact operation. Unrestricted actions need narrow scope, monitoring, and recovery. Product permission examples are not proof of a secure deployment. Different tools in one agent can use different authority profiles.
**What changes:** Maintain a tool-by-tool permission table with owner, allowed targets, approval thresholds, and tested failure behavior.

articles.title: EU AI Act versus NIST GenAI Profile: binding duties or risk guidance?
articles.author: Global AI News Editorial Desk

content_type_status.rationale: The completed draft was checked against the assigned editorial form.

content.dek: The EU AI Act creates legal obligations for actors within scope; NIST AI 600-1 organizes voluntary risk-management work. One does not substitute for the other.

body.heading: Two frameworks with different force
paragraphs: The EU AI Act and NIST’s Generative AI Profile both address AI risks, but they are not equivalent instruments. The AI Act is enacted European Union legislation with staged application dates and duties that depend on system classification, role, and applicable provision. NIST AI 600-1 is a cross-sectoral profile of the U.S. AI Risk Management Framework for generative AI. It offers organizations a way to structure governance, mapping, measurement, and management; it is not an EU regulation or a substitute for legal compliance. [@eu-aiact-article-113] [@eu-gpai-obligations] [@nist-genai-profile]

cells: Status
Enacted law, with staged dates
Voluntary risk-management profile
Primary purpose
Establish legal duties, prohibitions, and controls within scope
Help organizations identify and manage generative-AI risks
How to determine applicability
Check the system, provider/deployer role, use, market, classification, and specific provisions
Use the framework to decide what risks and controls fit the organization and use case
Structure
Provisions and obligations in the regulation, including duties for certain provider categories
Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage functions applied to generative AI
Enforcement or accountability
Legal enforcement under the regulation and relevant national/EU authorities
Organizational adoption and risk-management practice; no NIST enforcement mechanism in the profile
What it cannot do alone
Does not answer every implementation question without the applicable facts and guidance
Does not establish legal compliance or replace contracts and regulation

body.heading: Dates must be tied to the exact provision
paragraphs: The AI Act’s schedule is staged. Article 113 sets application dates for different chapters and provisions; the Commission’s GPAI guidance separately says provider obligations applied from 2 August 2025, Commission enforcement powers begin 2 August 2026, and pre-existing GPAI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 have until 2 August 2027 to comply. Certain high-risk systems under Annex I have a later transition to 2 August 2028. These dates answer different questions and should not be compressed into one general “AI Act start date.” [@eu-aiact-article-113] [@eu-gpai-guidelines] [@eu-gpai-obligations]

NIST AI 600-1 was approved in July 2024. It organizes risk-management actions through the AI RMF functions Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage and includes generative-AI considerations. It does not create a compliance deadline, a classification rule, or a regulator’s enforcement power. An organization may use it alongside the AI Act, but it still needs to map legal duties to its actual system and role. [@nist-genai-profile]

body.heading: Translate each into an operational plan
paragraphs: For an EU-facing product, first determine the AI Act’s scope and the organization’s role. Then identify system-specific obligations, applicable dates, evidence required, and who owns the control. Commission guidance can help interpret provider responsibilities, but enacted text governs the law. When the organization is also using the NIST Profile, it can use Govern to assign accountability, Map to define use and context, Measure to evaluate risks, and Manage to prioritize response. NIST is a complement for managing risk, not a legal interpretation service.

For a U.S. team that is not subject to the EU Act, NIST AI 600-1 can still help create a documented process for generative-AI risk. Its usefulness does not turn it into mandatory law. Other contracts, sector rules, state law, or organizational policies may still apply; the profile itself cannot determine all of them.

body.heading: Avoid false equivalence
paragraphs: A checklist match between NIST actions and an AI Act requirement does not show that one framework satisfies the other. A risk-management action might support evidence collection while a legal duty requires a specific process, documentation, or notice. Conversely, legal compliance does not guarantee that an organization has strong operational controls for every context. Keep a crosswalk with a separate column for the legal source, NIST action, owner, implementation evidence, and any unresolved legal question.

This comparison is informational, not legal advice. Teams should verify the current consolidated regulation, official guidance, and national implementation before making a compliance decision. The proposal for the EU KIDS Act is not included as a current legal obligation; Report 46 covers its proposal status separately. [@eu-aiact-article-113] [@eu-gpai-guidelines]

A practical crosswalk can be tested with one change-control question. Create the legal row first: system, organizational role, applicable provision, date, required evidence, and accountable owner. In a separate NIST row, record the use context, risk, measurement, response, and evidence. Link a shared artifact only where it genuinely supports both records; the existence of a risk assessment does not establish that a statutory requirement has been met. Mark obligations with no NIST analogue, and NIST actions that do not map to a legal duty, rather than forcing a one-to-one match. Date the source versions and route unresolved scope questions to legal review. This preserves the framework’s usefulness without converting it into a substitute for law.

Keep the two tracks current for different reasons. A change in the product, intended use, user population, provider/deployer role, or market can change the legal applicability analysis; a change in the system’s risk or operating context can change the NIST work. Record which event triggered each update and which owner approved it. Shared evidence may support both tracks, but each conclusion should retain its own source, status, and review date.
**Bottom line:** The AI Act defines binding duties for in-scope actors, while NIST AI 600-1 is a voluntary way to organize generative-AI risk work.
**Why it matters:** Treating guidance as law—or treating a risk checklist as proof of compliance—can leave both legal and operational gaps.

**Key takeaways:** Check AI Act scope and dates provision by provision. Keep Commission guidance distinct from enacted law. NIST’s Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage functions are a risk-management structure, not legal duties. A NIST crosswalk can support documentation but does not establish compliance. Seek qualified legal review for an organization-specific determination.
**What changes:** Maintain a dated legal applicability matrix and a separate NIST risk-control crosswalk.
